articles.title: The Documentary - Germany's rust belt revival - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Author Katja Hoyer, reports on a city which benefits from a new, green landscape
articles.body:
World Service , · 24 Oct 2026 , · 49 mins

In Germany’s Ruhr Valley, once the industrial heartland of the coal and steel industry, a remarkable transition into a modern, hi-tech economy is taking place. Based in Dortmund , the historian and author Katja Hoyer, reports on a city which benefits from a new, green landscape, excellent universities and a growing , youthful population - to say nothing of a world class football team. But for those left out of this brave new world the picture is not so bright. (Photo: The Phoenix Lake, originated and developed in the area of the former steel mill in Dortmund Hoesch-Hoerde. Credit: Klaus Rose/Getty Images)

articles.title: Crowds welcome Venezuela's María Machado after months in exile
articles.summary: The Venezuelan opposition leader spent more than 10 months in exile after escaping the country on a speedboat.
articles.body:
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home after more than 10 months in exile.

"I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return came after several prior efforts to re-enter the country came to no avail.

Machado attended Mass at a church in the state of Lara, and was surrounded by jubilant supporters.

Later, huge crowds lined the route of her journey through Caracas

The US seized her opponent, President Nicolás Maduro, last January. The move came a month after Machado escaped from Venezuela under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway.

The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as leader and she was sworn in as interim president.

articles.title: The Climate Question - How could climate change affect my health? - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Two doctors discuss the challenges for the medical sector from a warming world
articles.body:
World Service , · 25 Oct 2026 , · 26 mins

Climate change is having major health impacts around the world - which are only expected to increase as our planet gets warmer. These impacts range from heat stroke to the spread of tropical diseases, from hospitals losing power during extreme weather to the effect on our mental health. In a show first broadcast in 2025, Graihagh Jackson talks to two doctors from Malaysia and Egypt about the challenges the medical sector faces, as well as possible solutions and how healthcare must also address its own emissions problem. If you have a question or a comment, email us at theclimatequestion@bbc.com or leave a WhatsApp message at + 44 8000 321 721 Guests: Dr Jemilah Mahmoud, Executive Director, Sunway Centre for Planetary Health, Malaysia. articles.title: 62% of workers would rather their kids become electricians than software developers: How AI anxiety may be reshaping career choices
articles.summary: A new survey shows how parents are approaching the job talk with their kids in the age of artificial intelligence.
articles.body:
Forget computer science degrees; most parents would prefer that their kids become electricians rather than software developers.

That's according to a new survey from Careerminds , a global workforce solutions provider, that highlights anxiety over how AI might affect job opportunities and security, changing attitudes about what makes a good, satisfying job and how parents feel about their kids' futures.

It comes as young adults — especially Gen Zers — are increasingly enrolling in trade schools instead of (or in addition to) pursuing four-year college degrees.

With AI already reshaping so many industries, what do parents want for their children's future — and how are they preparing them for it? Yahoo spoke to an expert who has been asking them.

Careerminds surveyed more than 3,000 workers who said they are happy and secure in their current jobs about how worried they are that they could be replaced or affected by AI.

Nurses were the most confident about the future of their careers in the coming decade, with 81% saying they felt very or somewhat secure. They were closely followed by HVAC technicians (80%), electricians, dentists and auto mechanics (78% in each group). Notably, of the top 10 most secure job categories, only two — dentist and physical therapist — require advanced degrees (though some nursing positions, including nurse practitioners, require postgraduate education).

Job security rivals income when it comes to many workers' priorities, according to the survey results. More than 40% said they would take a pay cut today to guarantee that their job would never be replaced by AI. And " email jobs " or white-collar work might not be as enviable as it once was. More than three-quarters of survey respondents said they felt sorry for those working in fields that are at risk of AI replacement.

When asked to choose whether they'd want their children to become electricians or software developers, the majority — 62% — chose the skilled trade.

That said, it's unclear whether the survey respondents included people who work in tech, and that's exactly who Katie Shilton is interviewing for her research. The University of Maryland professor studies and teaches technology, and is compiling data from her conversations with parents in tech who are talking to their kids about the future of work. The research is ongoing, but so far, she says parents aren't ruling out careers in their industry or dissuading their kids from pursuing them. But they're considering other options too.

"These are fairly wealthy people, so I've been surprised by how open they seem to many kinds of careers" for their children, Shilton says. "People have absolutely brought up blue-collar jobs as a possibility for their kids."

Shilton is also interviewing people who have a more detailed picture of what work in tech looks like. Sure, they tell her, coding itself may not be the golden ticket it once was, but tech isn't going anywhere, and neither are jobs in the industry. But there are other options on the table.

The 'toolbelt generation' shift has already begun

Gen Z is notoriously money-conscious , and they're making moves to improve their job security in the age of AI. With or without college degrees , significant shares of Zoomers are considering or already working in blue-collar jobs or skilled trades. Trade schools are seeing a surge in enrollment, especially among Gen Zers. And AI anxiety is an oft-cited motivator, making jobs like welding look more future-proof than white-collar roles. And there's data to back up their decisions; the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment growth for HVAC technicians , electricians and plumbers in the coming years.

But if the young adults of today — or the children who will be entering the job market in the coming years — really want stability, they should perhaps consider nursing. Jobs in the health care sector are expected to see the most growth and are among the least likely to be replaced by an AI agent .

How parents are future-proofing their kids

It's worth noting that Careerminds didn't ask parents which career they'd most like for their children to choose. Instead, participants were just given the choice of software developer or electrician. Shilton notes, too, that in reality parents aren't always choosing their kids' careers for them. Their efforts to prepare them for the future are more nuanced. But they do include encouraging their children to think critically about AI and technology in general.

She also says that parents aren't necessarily expecting their kids to follow in their footsteps. "I suspect that is because of this trait that these are folks that didn't do what their parents wanted them to do," explains Shilton. "Many of their parents specifically wanted them to go into medicine or finance, and they chose differently."

And AI isn't the whole story. Parents are "anxious but not panicked" about how machine learning and large language models will alter their own careers as well as their children's future work, Shilton says. They just don't know what the employment picture will look like by the time their kids reach the job market.

Which is why, Shilton says, a big part of parents' efforts to prepare their kids for the future is to teach them to be nimble and open to many possibilities.

"People are saying, 'I just want my kid to be resilient and change a lot in their career. I want them to be flexible and have a broad set of skills so that they can navigate that change,'" says Shilton.

images.caption: Amid anxiety over AI's threat to tech careers, a survey found that many parents would prefer to see their kids learn to be electricians rather than software developers.

articles.title: Trump’s DOJ told a judge how to rule. Then it pulled her from court.
articles.summary: THE JUDGE HAD JUST CALLED COURT TO ORDER on that winter morning, and already, a dozen attorneys waited on her TV screen, each with an urgent request. Their c...
articles.body:
Trump’s DOJ told a judge how to rule. Then it pulled her from court.

THE JUDGE HAD JUST CALLED COURT TO ORDER on that winter morning, and already, a dozen attorneys waited on her TV screen, each with an urgent request. Their clients, all locked up and facing deportation, needed hearing dates scheduled or bond requests considered. As always, the judge had prepared for every case days earlier, because almost nothing happened in Courtroom 15 that she didn't anticipate.

Then the door behind her swung open, thudding against the wall. In walked her supervisor.

"Are you on the record?" he asked, questioning whether she was in session.

Karen Donoso Stevens was in session, and she was certain he knew it. The judge held up a finger - wait - as she announced a recess inside the Annandale Immigration Court.

A Homeland Security attorney at the prosecution table watched in silence, as did her legal assistant.

She drew a long breath, then stood in the black robe she'd worn for nearly a decade, its cloth fraying at the elbow.

Here we go , the judge thought, certain she was about to be fired.

In the hallway, she recalled, her supervisor said he'd been instructed to pull her from court.

It was Jan. 14, one year into the most tumultuous period in the U.S. immigration court's history. President Donald Trump had inherited what was widely seen as a broken system. Exacerbated by an influx of migrants under President Joe Biden, its backlog exceeded 4 million unresolved cases, and Trump's administration had vowed to address it.

The public broadly supported tighter border security before his election, though the aggressive crackdown that followed alienated many voters, recent polls show. As the administration stripped protections from asylum seekers and dispatched thousands of ICE agents onto American streets, leading to more detentions and deportations, two U.S. citizens were killed by federal officers in Minneapolis, igniting a backlash.

But no cog in Trump's effort to expel millions of "illegal aliens" was more essential - and less familiar to the public - than the immigration courts that decide who stays and who goes.

The sprawling system doesn't operate like most courts. It exists within the Justice Department, which is overseen by the attorney general and, ultimately, the president. Nevertheless, it is obligated to afford migrants due process and manage cases according to the law, nothing else.

And yet, in the first year of Trump's second term, the Justice Department fired some 100 of the country's roughly 700 immigration judges and began to replace them with what the administration called "deportation judges."

Donoso Stevens, 53, should have been insulated from the institutional chaos, according to fellow judges and attorneys whose cases she oversaw. Before joining the bench in 2016, she'd spent a decade at Homeland Security, earning a reputation as a formidable prosecutor. She was Annandale's most tenured "detained judge," one of three who decided what to do with migrants in custody, the court's highest-stakes cases.

Every year, Donoso Stevens had denied asylum in more than half the applications that came before her, a record consistently in line with national averages. She hadn't resisted case quotas imposed by the first Trump administration and seldom took sick leave. She never fell behind on her docket.

But on that morning in Northern Virginia, she feared none of it mattered. By then, Donoso Stevens said, another supervisor had already ordered her to reverse four rulings at the direction of unidentified "higher-ups," a violation of judicial authority she once considered inconceivable. The interference, she said, had only escalated since.

The allegations, which she's sharing publicly for the first time because of her deep concern for the court's integrity, were corroborated by her extensive contemporaneous notes as well as colleagues, family and private attorneys interviewed by The Washington Post. They contradict Trump officials' insistence to the public and to The Post that - as required by law - immigration judges serve under the administration as independent arbiters of justice.

Outside her courtroom, Donoso Stevens tried to make sense of what was happening. She would remain on the bench but no longer oversee cases for migrants in detention, she was told by Robert K. Lundberg, Annandale's acting assistant chief immigration judge, a largely administrative role he'd been moved into a week earlier.

Donoso Stevens asked if she could finish the hearing. He said no, she recalled: "You're not allowed to go back and say what happened."

The judge returned to court and turned on her camera.

"I've been told I'm no longer able to finish these hearings," she said, her voice quavering.

On the video call, she heard attorneys gasp. Then the judge walked out. Word spread through the legal community within minutes. Many assumed she'd been fired.

Back in the hallway, Donoso Stevens saw Lundberg escorting her replacement, a man she'd trained and mentored, toward her courtroom. He immediately took over her docket, including a prominent case that legal experts had said could set a precedent with sweeping consequences for tens of thousands of Afghans seeking refuge in the United States.

Donoso Stevens returned to her office and removed her robe. She wept.

In the hours that followed, colleagues and friends tried to console her. At least, they said, she still had a job. But the judge, who so often preached that her only duty was to follow the law, asked herself: What would she have to do to keep it?

DONOSO STEVENS BEGAN TO WORRY, she said, on the 26th day of Trump's second term. She was in the car with her husband, headed home from a Valentine's Day dinner, when her phone buzzed, then kept buzzing.

"No way," Donoso Stevens blurted as she read the texts.

Her supervisor, Rebecca Walters, had been fired, one of seven assistant chief immigration judges dismissed that day. Appointed under Biden, Walters was credited with dramatically improving Annandale's case-completion numbers, an achievement that colleagues hoped would ingratiate her with a Trump administration that had imposed quotas during his first term.

Dozens of other terminations soon followed, spotlighting what many legal experts have called a systemic flaw in the court system: Unlike federal judges protected from political retaliation by lifetime tenures and the constitutional separation of powers, immigration judges work for the executive branch.

No administration had ever carried out a purge at this scale. Trump officials asserted they had every right to banish, as the White House put it, "activist judges who slow-walked deportations and granted asylum at sky-high rates." But even as the expulsions instilled what surviving judges in private conversation began to call a "culture of intimidation," the Justice Department insisted it would not interfere with their rulings.

"They are required to adjudicate cases independently and impartially without favor to either party," Sirce E. Owen, appointed under Trump as acting director of the Executive Office for Immigration Review, wrote in a memo last summer. Owen declared that no one in the executive office, the agency that oversees the entire immigration court system, can "direct any adjudicator to rule in a particular way" before appeals are settled.

Donoso Stevens wanted that to be true, because the institution had become central to her identity. She'd endured a two-year application process before being appointed to the bench a decade earlier by Democratic Attorney General Loretta E. Lynch. The job was the zenith of her career and, she thought, its destination. She found purpose in studying the law and applying it, even if that meant ordering the deportation of people whose pleas for sanctuary devastated her.

She'd believed in the sanctity of America's legal system since well before she swore an oath to the Constitution. Donoso Stevens decided to become an attorney when she read "To Kill a Mockingbird" as a high school junior. The ideals of truth and justice appealed to her, as did getting paid to persuade people she was right. The middle child of Ecuadorian immigrants in the Chicago suburbs, she'd always served as her siblings' advocate, negotiating punishments and bedtimes. When she turned 17, her dad ordered a vanity plate for the pickup they shared: "2 B LWYR."

She met her eventual husband, Damon Stevens, when they competed against each other in moot court at Michigan State University College of Law. She won.

"She's got an edge," he said, recalling how her diminutive stature, at 5-foot-3, could mislead. "If you're opposing her, she's not a wallflower."

After graduation, Donoso Stevens prosecuted misdemeanor assaults and DUIs in a Chicago criminal court until she followed her husband to California, where he'd been stationed as a judge advocate in the Marine Corps. Amid cross-country moves, she had two kids and worked at a nonprofit to help children who'd arrived in the U.S. without their parents. In 2007, she joined Homeland Security as a prosecutor.

"I remember how proud I was to be a federal employee," said Donoso Stevens, whose parents had instilled a deep allegiance to the country that gave them citizenship. "I never saw myself doing the law for money."

She was especially tenacious in trying to deport immigrants accused of domestic violence or harming kids, according to defense lawyers, who noted they never found her unreasonable.

"She was agreeable when there was room to agree," said Anam Petit, then a private attorney who later served as a judge before being fired without cause last year. "She was always thoughtful."

In liberal Washington, Donoso Stevens knew that many people considered her job distasteful because it often meant fighting to deny immigrants a home in the United States. Weary of being asked how she could sleep at night, she stopped revealing what she did for a living.

"I work for the government," she'd say, and nothing more.

Back then, she said, Homeland Security attorneys weren't evaluated on wins and losses. If immigrants proved they deserved asylum, she didn't fight them.

Ricky Malik once represented an attorney from El Salvador whose family had been terrorized after the woman investigated gang members. In court, Donoso Stevens confirmed the story, then told the judge that Homeland Security did not oppose her application.

"Justice, that was her main goal," Malik said. "Not just, 'I'm going to win every case, and I'm going to have a body count.'"

Still, when she was appointed to the bench, at the time an uncommon transition for a Homeland Security attorney, Malik and other defense lawyers protested. How, they asked, could she rule with impartiality when former colleagues sat at the prosecution table?

"This is unfair," he said, before she began overseeing his cases. As the years passed, Malik said, he found in her what he wanted most from every judge: She followed the law.

HOW TO FOLLOW THE LAW got more complicated on a Friday afternoon in September 2025. In a 14-page ruling, the Board of Immigration Appeals, stocked with members appointed under Trump, stripped judges of a power they had exercised for decades.

Undocumented immigrants who weren't apprehended until after they entered the country had long been allowed to request bond, leaving judges to decide whether it was safe to release them as their cases proceeded. Suddenly, the board decided that anyone who came unlawfully should remain jailed, even those with clean records and family ties.

Donoso Stevens disagreed with the board's legal interpretation, but her view, she said, made no difference. She treated its decisions as the mandates they are.

Still, she and other judges quickly spotted a potentially critical omission: The opinion failed to account for children who came to the United States without a parent or guardian and had since reached adulthood, a group that, in their view, fell under distinct legal guidelines.

Less than two weeks later, four such people asked Donoso Stevens to release them. She studied the law and consulted with colleagues, then decided the immigrants were eligible. She granted bonds.

On Sept. 17, Annandale's then-acting assistant chief, Eric Dillow, called her.

"Dillow ... said bond is a hot topic. Wanted to discuss bond decisions," Donoso Stevens jotted in a green steno pad reviewed by The Post. He told her he knew about the four cases and had just emailed her a separate ruling that, he believed, meant she could have denied bond.

When Donoso Stevens pressed him, she said, Dillow acknowledged the four cases had been "elevated" to him. He didn't say by whom, and she neglected to ask. Nevertheless, it was a stunning disclosure. As far as she knew, none of her rulings had ever been reported to a supervisor.

She hung up and read the ruling Dillow had sent, then he called back. From her office, Donoso Stevens told him she could see the merits of the argument, even though it came from a federal court in New York that couldn't require her or any other immigration judge in Virginia to follow it.

She told him Homeland Security should follow legal protocol: The department could either file a motion asking her to reconsider or request that the appellate board intervene. He agreed, according to her notes, but called back a few minutes later.

Suspicious, she allowed another judge who had come to her office to listen in.

"He said higher-ups said I had to vacate my decs sua sponte," Donoso Stevens wrote in a note that abbreviated "decisions" and used a Latin phrase that refers to judges reversing their own rulings unprompted.

Dillow did not name the "higher-ups." Donoso Stevens pushed for an explanation: "Why can't DHS file a motion to reconsider?"

"Oh no," he replied. "They're not going to do that."

"Is this our red line?" Donoso Stevens asked the other judge. The colleague, to whom The Post granted anonymity because they fear professional retaliation, confirmed the details of the call.

To Donoso Stevens, Dillow had not only told her how to rule, directly violating the executive office's vow of judicial independence, he'd implied that Homeland Security had ordered the court system to acquiesce.

The Post described the allegation to three legal experts, and all of them condemned it as unacceptable.

"It's an example of direct interference in an immigration judge's handling of a case," said Jill E. Family, a professor at Widener University Commonwealth Law School. "That is a very disturbing affront on the basic norms of our legal system."

The Post sent a detailed list of questions to the Justice Department and Homeland Security as well as Dillow, Lundberg and every other government official Donoso Stevens named in her account of what happened. None responded to the allegations.

"DOJ's approach is to impartially adjudicate cases as efficiently as possible in accordance with the law and evidence," an executive office spokesperson wrote in a statement. "It does not view adjudications in terms of outcomes and does not have a stake in any particular outcome."

Donoso Stevens said she considered refusing Dillow's order to overturn her rulings. But because she conceded that the New York case offered a reasonable counterargument, the judge reluctantly agreed to reverse herself, she said, a choice she still debates.

A week later, after backlash over a push to rapidly dismiss cases and expedite arrests, the executive office insisted again that the court had total independence. It issued a memo that appeared in conflict with Dillow's edict: No one in its leadership "may direct an Immigration Judge to decide a case in a particular way."

But in private, leadership continued to undermine its public pronouncements.

On Nov. 18, Teresa L. Riley, appointed under Trump to lead the country's entire immigration court system, emailed Donoso Stevens, demanding justification for why she'd granted bond in six other cases. Donoso Stevens said she couldn't provide the message to The Post because of pending litigation, but she described it.

When Dillow called to discuss Riley's email, Donoso Stevens told him she hadn't acted unilaterally. Federal courts had ordered bond hearings in all six of her cases, in response to habeas corpus petitions challenging the government's legal right to keep migrants locked up. Dillow told Donoso Stevens he understood, she said, and promised to convey her account to his bosses. Riley, who didn't reply to a request for comment, never followed up with Donoso Stevens.

The bond issue seemed to recede until early January, when Lundberg replaced Dillow as Annandale's acting assistant chief.

Within a day or two, Lundberg appeared in her office doorway.

"Judge, just because habeas hearings are ordered doesn't mean you have to grant bond," she said he told her. Donoso Stevens interpreted that as an instruction to conduct "show" hearings, she said, where the outcomes for immigrants would be predetermined.

"If bond is warranted - if they prove they're not a danger or a flight risk - then I'm going to grant bond," the judge said she told him.

He looked at her, she said, and walked away, silent.

Less than a week later, he opened the door to her courtroom and asked if she was on the record.

NEWS OF DONOSO STEVENS'S DEMOTION stunned private lawyers and dismayed fellow judges, but the most immediate effects fell on the immigrants who would have appeared before her.

Since the start of Trump's second presidency, Donoso Stevens had denied about 85 percent of her asylum claims, according to a Post analysis of Justice Department data. She largely ascribed the highest rate of her career to how much more difficult the board's mandates made it to approve applications. Her replacement, Richard VanVeldhuisen, who joined the bench in 2023 and had never overseen a docket of detained immigrants, denied about 95 percent in his new assignment.

His rate mirrors the court's soaring national averages in 2026. While the board's decrees are limiting, legal experts say, judges have succumbed to immense pressure from the Trump administration to deny applications.

"It is a hurricane-force wind against judicial independence," said Dana Leigh Marks, a former immigration judge who, since retiring after 35 years, has become a fierce Trump critic. "Everybody has a different tolerance point."

The most high-profile asylum case VanVeldhuisen inherited from Donoso Stevens was that of an Afghan who, after supporting the United States' cause in his home country, escaped with his wife on a U.S. military plane as American troops withdrew in 2021. In July of last year, ICE officers arrested the man, whom The Post is identifying as H out of concern for his safety, on his way to work at an accounting firm.

In court, Homeland Security attorneys argued to Donoso Stevens that H, who has never been charged with a crime, could be safely sent back, despite the Taliban's brutal regime. If the courts accepted that rationale, legal experts suspected it could help the agency expel thousands of other Afghans.

Homeland Security later submitted surprise evidence: an unsigned FBI memo that accused H of no wrongdoing but described him as "a potential threat" because of distant relatives who were associated with terrorist groups. Donoso Stevens pressed the prosecutor for more details on the memo, but he provided none, saying his "chain of command" had given it to him.

Donoso Stevens can't share how she would have ruled, she said, but there were signs in court that she found the government's case unconvincing, noting that H, who'd answered hundreds of questions under oath, had not "testified to anything that would make him a national security interest."

After Homeland Security announced the FBI had yet to finish his background check, a frustrated Donoso Stevens acknowledged that, by law, she didn't have the option to grant the father of two asylum until he was cleared by the bureau, which the Justice Department also oversees. A prosecutor reminded the judge she could reject H's application at any time. She declined.

The clearance arrived three months later, in January - just nine days after Donoso Stevens was removed from the case.

On Feb. 18, VanVeldhuisen, who had never consulted with her about it or held a hearing on H's case, ordered him to be sent back to Afghanistan.

The judge wrote that because of H's relatives, he "may pose a danger to the national security." In a footnote, VanVeldhuisen, who did not respond to a request for comment, mentioned that the judge "formerly assigned to this case is unavailable to complete" it. Donoso Stevens remained on the bench, in a courtroom not far from his own.

H's attorney filed a habeas corpus petition to the Eastern District of Virginia, but a Trump-appointed judge denied it, citing, among other things, VanVeldhuisen's conclusion that H may be a danger, "which this Court cannot second-guess."

OVER AND OVER, TRUMP OFFICIALS have demanded more productivity from immigration judges. His first administration asserted that "efficient adjudication" served "the national interest" and instituted quotas. His second administration has set strict case-completion deadlines "to address the substantial backlog exacerbated by prior leadership."

"No more endless delays," the White House declared. "Only results."

Donoso Stevens believed in results, too. That's what so infuriated her one February morning after her demotion when she discovered seven white cardboard boxes outside her chambers. The executive office had instructed judges to rule on 95 percent of their motions within 30 days. Now, beside her door, she found more than 100 of VanVeldhuisen's unresolved filings - all from Homeland Security and all at least six months old.

Donoso Stevens struggled to understand how ignoring the government's legal requests served its own goal of "efficient adjudication."

And she was suddenly responsible for every one of them.

"This is f---ing unbelievable," she said to herself.

Donoso Stevens, who, in her new role, had already taken on about a thousand asylum applications from immigrants not in detention, demanded an explanation from Lundberg's staff. When none came, she requested a meeting. The judge pitched him on ways to make Annandale more efficient, she said, but the discussion in early March, which included other administrators, quickly turned combative.

"So you're basically telling me all the things I've done wrong," she recalled him snapping.

Donoso Stevens left the meeting shaken and angry. On March 6, in an email she read parts of to The Post, the judge followed up on their discussion.

"Annandale Immigration Court and the broader EOIR," she wrote, "are understandably and correctly under significant pressure from DOJ and the American people to be as efficient as possible in significantly reducing the longstanding backlog of cases."

She created a spreadsheet for every outstanding motion and, over two months, cleared them all. On April 20, Lundberg signed her performance review, grading her "satisfactory," the highest possible rating. In the accompanying email, she said, he thanked her for her work on the motions. The same day, she wrote in her notes, he stopped her in the hallway: "Said I was doing a great job completing cases."

On May 21, Donoso Stevens hurried out of the courthouse just after lunch for a doctor's appointment. A mammogram had spotted a mass, and she needed another test to determine whether she had cancer. Regardless of the diagnosis, she intended to head back to court for an afternoon hearing.

After the scan, she was sent to a waiting room while a doctor studied the result. There, in her gown, she noticed a text from Lundberg.

"Good afternoon. The EOIR Director forwarded to me the Notice of Termination that you received this morning," he wrote at 2:35 p.m. "I looked for you but you had left the court."

"I don't know what you are talking about," she replied.

Then the doctor called her in: She didn't have cancer.

On her drive back to court, she realized the Trump administration had fired her nine months before she would have become eligible for her pension.

Lundberg met her in the lobby. He refused to let her inside.

ONE THURSDAY MORNING LAST MONTH , Donoso Stevens made a vanilla latte and settled onto her living room couch. Wearing a sweatshirt and yoga pants, she tried to talk her husband into a shopping trip, because she had little else to do. Her black robe sat folded in a bedroom dresser.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit, which has jurisdiction over Annandale's cases, had rejected the administration's legal argument to deny bond hearings to every immigrant who entered the country unlawfully.

It was the latest in a series of 11 federal appellate courts that had weighed in on the bond question, nine of them deciding against the government. The Supreme Court is expected to settle it by June, but as the appeals have plodded through the system, thousands of migrants have agreed to leave the country rather than wait behind bars.

For Donoso Stevens, the September ruling affirmed her resolve to hold bona fide bond hearings, despite the pressure not to. As she read the 86-page decision, the texts popping up on her phone all delivered a version of the same message: You were right .

Former colleagues praised the principled commitment they suspected had cost Donoso Stevens her career.

Lundberg never provided a reason for her dismissal. Like most judges, her termination letter cited "Article II of the Constitution," a reference to the executive branch's powers.

"EOIR continually evaluates all immigration judges, regardless of background, on factors such as conduct, impartiality/bias, adherence to the law, productivity/performance, and professionalism," a spokesperson wrote in a statement that noted the executive office doesn't comment on personnel matters, "to include a disgruntled former employee's allegations against the agency."

Donoso Stevens wouldn't speculate on her firing because she's appealed it, making her one of at least a dozen former immigration judges across the country who argue they were unlawfully dismissed. A federal appeals court in D.C. will soon hear oral arguments on the central case hers could hinge on, but ultimately, the Supreme Court may settle that issue as well.

In the meantime, legal experts say the Justice Department's transformation of the immigration court has set a precedent that could upend the system each time a new president takes office: more mass firings, more ideological hirings, more pressure to appease whoever is in charge.

Democrats in both the Senate and House have introduced bills that would remove the court from the executive branch, affording it true independence, but without Republican support, the legislation has little chance of passage.

"We were public servants, and I feel like something was taken from me, something that I loved," Donoso Stevens said. "The argument the administration is making is that, under Article II, we can be fired for any reason. And if we allow that, then we are basically becoming de facto political appointees."

FIVE WEEKS LATER, H, the Afghan denied asylum by Donoso Stevens's replacement, returned to immigration court. The U.S. government - the same one that had worked for months to deny immigrants like him bond - had requested a hearing to decide whether he should be released.

It didn't say why. H's attorney, Justice Haynes, suspected Homeland Security wanted to preempt any new habeas petitions prompted by the 4th Circuit's bond decision.

By then, H, 30, had lost faith in the American legal system. He couldn't bear what would happen to his children in Afghanistan if he were sent back, but the stress of staying, and fighting, was so intense his hair had begun to fall out. His brother, a delivery driver who had served as an interpreter for the U.S. Army, struggled to cover a mortgage while he supported two families. H's wife quit her English classes and had to visit local food banks every week. His daughter, 4, had stopped asking when her dad would come home.

Now H, eyes bloodshot and baggy, watched on a video screen as one of his attorneys argued that, after 15 months in ICE detention, he should be released while his appeals proceed. The lawyer reviewed his clean record, professional résumé, community support, love for his kids and devotion to his new country.

Then, from the prosecutor's table, a Homeland Security attorney reminded the court of the ruling from VanVeldhuisen, who had decided in February that H was a national security risk.

If not for that decision, the judge acknowledged, she would release him.

"But I can't undo what another judge already found," she said. "My hands are really tied."

So she denied bond. As H returned to his cell, he once more imagined how differently his life might have unfolded if the case had been decided all those months ago by Donoso Stevens.

"I think the first judge I had," H said later, "she was a victim of this politics."

"She was fair," he added, because she had listened to his story and scrutinized the facts and challenged the government, as he always thought judges in America were supposed to do.

He's been told it could take another year for the courts to decide whether to let him go back to his family, or send him to the Taliban.

Emmanuel Martinez contributed to this report.

articles.title: 'É preciso respeitar o resultado das urnas', afirma João Doria após vitória de Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: A manifestação ocorre dois dias depois do ex-governador de São Paulo declarar apoio a Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no segundo turno da eleição presidencial.
articles.summary: A manifestação ocorre dois dias depois do ex-governador de São Paulo declarar apoio a Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no segundo turno da eleição presidencial.
articles.body:
Foto de arquivo de 08/10/2018 de João Doria, na época candidato ao governo de São Paulo pelo PSDB, durante entrevista exclusiva para o Grupo Estado, na capital paulista. — Foto: WERTHER SANTANA/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

O ex-governador de São Paulo João Doria publicou nas redes sociais, na manhã desta segunda-feira (26), uma mensagem em que reconhece a vitória de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) na disputa pela Presidência da República e defende o respeito ao resultado das urnas.

A manifestação ocorre dois dias depois de Doria declarar apoio a Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no segundo turno da eleição presidencial.

No domingo (25), em uma disputa acirrada e marcada por uma virada inédita, Lula foi reeleito presidente da República ao obter 64.256.232 votos, contra 59.826.041 votos de Flávio .

"É preciso respeitar o resultado das urnas. Mesmo com tristeza, é necessário reconhecer a vitória de Lula e torcer para que ele não faça um governo de ódio e ressentimento, mas tenha grandeza para governar para todos os brasileiros", escreveu Doria.

Na publicação, o ex-governador também afirmou que o país precisa de paz e defendeu a democracia.

"O que o Brasil mais precisa, além de um bom governo, é de paz. Um país dividido não progride, não encontra seu caminho, nem alcança o desenvolvimento econômico e social. Não podemos abandonar a democracia e seus valores", disse.

Doria ainda classificou a disputa presidencial como a mais acirrada da história do país. "Esta foi a mais acirrada das eleições presidenciais da história. Que sirva de lição para todos nós."

articles.title: Farma Conde lança campanha com R$ 150 mil em prêmios aos clientes | G1
articles.standfirst: Com o tema “É Hora de Ganhar”, rede de farmácias lança promoção especial de aniversário com uma roleta premiada e sorteios pela Loteria Federal
articles.summary: Com o tema “É Hora de Ganhar”, rede de farmácias lança promoção especial de aniversário com uma roleta premiada e sorteios pela Loteria Federal
articles.body:
A Farma Conde celebra seus 33 anos de história com uma campanha especial que coloca os clientes no centro das comemorações. Com o tema “É Hora de Ganhar”, a rede de farmácias lançou uma promoção que vai distribuir R$ 150 mil em prêmios, reunindo uma roleta digital premiada e sorteios pela Loteria Federal, que prometem tornar a experiência de compra ainda mais especial.

A iniciativa acontece até 22 de dezembro e foi desenvolvida para agradecer a confiança dos consumidores que fazem parte da trajetória da empresa. Ao todo, serão disponibilizados 926 prêmios, distribuídos por meio de duas modalidades promocionais: sorteios e premiações pela roleta digital.

Entre os destaques estão 50 prêmios de R$ 1 mil, que serão sorteados ao longo da campanha, além de 876 prêmios disponibilizados na dinâmica da roleta, sendo 845 vale-compras de R$ 100 e outros 31 de R$ 500.

Fundada em 1993, em Ubatuba, no Litoral Norte de São Paulo, a Farma Conde construiu uma trajetória de crescimento mantendo o cuidado com as pessoas como um dos principais valores da marca. Agora, a comemoração de mais um aniversário se transforma em uma oportunidade de aproximar ainda mais a empresa de seus consumidores.

Para Cláudia Conde, farmacêutica e fundadora da Farma Conde, a campanha representa uma forma de reconhecer o papel dos clientes na construção dessa história.

“Completar 33 anos é uma conquista muito especial para todos nós. A Farma Conde nasceu com o propósito de cuidar das pessoas, e cada cliente que confia no nosso trabalho faz parte dessa trajetória. Queremos que essa comemoração também seja deles. Por isso, preparamos uma campanha com muitas oportunidades de ganhar, como uma forma de agradecer por todos esses anos de confiança e carinho”, destaca Cláudia Conde.

A dinâmica foi pensada para permitir que os consumidores participem tanto dos sorteios quanto da roleta premiada.

Nas compras a partir de R$ 33 em produtos participantes não medicamentos, realizadas nas unidades da Farma Conde, o consumidor tem direito a um Giro da Sorte na roleta digital e a um número da sorte para concorrer aos sorteios de R$ 1 mil, desde que cumpra as condições previstas nos regulamentos.

Para participar, é necessário acessar o site oficial da campanha ( ), realizar o cadastro e registrar o cupom fiscal da compra. Após a validação das informações, o participante poderá utilizar seu giro na roleta e consultar os números da sorte recebidos.

A promoção também conta com produtos aceleradores de marcas selecionadas. Ao incluir pelo menos um desses itens em uma compra elegível, o consumidor recebe um número da sorte adicional, ampliando suas oportunidades nos sorteios. Cada compra pode gerar até dois números da sorte e um giro na roleta, conforme os regulamentos.

Mais do que celebrar uma data, a campanha reforça a relação de proximidade que a Farma Conde construiu com seus consumidores ao longo de mais de três décadas.

A proposta é transformar o aniversário da rede em uma experiência de participação e premiação, valorizando quem acompanha o crescimento da empresa e faz parte de sua história.

Os sorteios serão realizados em cinco etapas, com dez ganhadores de R$ 1 mil em cada uma delas. As apurações estão programadas em datas especificas, conforme os resultados das extrações da Loteria Federal previstas nos regulamentos.

A campanha é válida para maiores de 18 anos, com CPF regular, e contempla exclusivamente os produtos participantes. Medicamentos não são elegíveis para a promoção e não entram no cálculo do valor mínimo para participação.

Todas as informações, a relação de produtos participantes, as regras da roleta premiada e os regulamentos completos estão disponíveis no site oficial:

articles.title: Eduardo Leite parabeniza Lula por vitória e pede respeito ao resultado | G1
articles.standfirst: Governador do Rio Grande do Sul, que optou por neutralidade no segundo turno, usou as redes sociais para pedir que o momento seja de serenidade e de "estender as mãos".
articles.summary: Governador do Rio Grande do Sul, que optou por neutralidade no segundo turno, usou as redes sociais para pedir que o momento seja de serenidade e de "estender as mãos"
articles.body:
O governador do Rio Grande do Sul, Eduardo Leite (PSD), parabenizou Lula pela vitória neste domingo (25) e pediu que todos respeitassem o resultado das eleições. Leite não revelou em quem votou no 2º turno da eleição presidencial e optou por não apoiar nenhum dos candidatos .

Após a reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) , ele usou as redes sociais para falar sobre o resultado.

"Aos que comemoram, que a alegria não se transforme em provocação ou humilhação. Aos que estão frustrados com o resultado, que possam compreendê-lo com serenidade e respeito à vontade expressa nas urnas."

Leite destacou que, apesar das diferenças, o momento é de "estender as mãos e fazer gestos em direção a todos os brasileiros". "As nossas diferenças políticas continuarão existindo, e isso é próprio da democracia", afirma.

Com 51,79% dos votos, Lula derrotou Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). Governador eleito no RS, Luciano Zucco apoiou o candidato do partido na eleição presidencial .

Eduardo Leite — Foto: Mauricio Tonetto/Palácio Piratini

"Cumprimento o presidente Lula pela vitória e desejo êxito na missão de conduzir o Brasil nos próximos quatro anos.

Aos que comemoram, que a alegria não se transforme em provocação ou humilhação. Aos que estão frustrados com o resultado, que possam compreendê-lo com serenidade e respeito à vontade expressa nas urnas.

Agora é hora de estender as mãos e fazer gestos em direção a todos os brasileiros. As nossas diferenças políticas continuarão existindo, e isso é próprio da democracia. Mas, acima delas, somos todos brasileiros e devemos torcer para que o Brasil vá bem.

Que o novo governo tenha sabedoria para reconhecer a divisão do país, governar para todos e trabalhar pela união, pela paz e pelo futuro da nossa gente."

articles.title: Imagens de drone mostram alagamentos na Rua do Porto em Piracicaba  | G1
articles.standfirst: Cidade registrou 70,33 milímetros de chuva nas últimas 24 horas, segundo Defesa Civil. Avenida Beira Rio e Jaime Pereira foram bloqueadas.
articles.summary: A cheia do Rio Piracicaba alagou a Rua do Porto e bloqueou vias após a cidade registrar o dobro da chuva esperada para todo o mês de outubro.
articles.body:
Imagens feitas por drone mostram a dimensão dos alagamentos na região da Rua do Porto e Bongue em Piracicaba (SP) após o Rio Piracicaba transbordar com as chuvas intensas registradas na cidade. Assista, acima.

Na manhã desta segunda-feira (26), trechos alagados da Rua do Porto em Piracicaba (SP) seguem interditados devido extravasamento do Rio Piracicaba neste domingo (25). A Prefeitura informou o manancial chegou a 5,91 metros.

As águas começaram a baixar, mas vias ficaram completamente submersas. Na Estrada do Bongue também houve transtornos e queda de árvores.

Imagens de drone registram cenário do Rio Piracicaba na Rua do Porto — Foto: Marcio Silveira/EPTV

Imagens de drone registram alagamentos na Rua do Porto em Piracicaba — Foto: Marcio Silveira/ EPTV

A água alcançava a cintura das pessoas que enfrentavam as enchentes. O cenário, apesar de não ser novo para quem vive na região ainda causa transtornos e assusta.

O manancial que leva o nome da cidade transborda ao alcançar 4,70 metros. A cidade registrou mais de 70 milímetros de chuvas em 24 horas.

Rio Piracicaba atingiu 5,91 metros durante as chuvas — Foto: Helen Sacconi/EPTV

No domingo (25), o Rio Piracicaba alcançou 4,96 metros por volta das 9h40, atingindo nível de extravasamento do manancial na região da Rua do Porto.

Alguns moradores de casas próximas ao Rio Piracicaba se previniram e ergueram os móveis antes que às águas da mananciam invadissem os imóveis. As cheias são recorrentes no trecho, mas geralmente ocorrem entre dezembro e janeiro. Dessa vez, a situação se adiantou, em outubro.

O morador Rodrigo Ferreira tem uma casa em rua da região que foi totalmente invadida pela água do Rio Piracicaba.

O instrutor contou que foi ajudar o irmão a levantar os móveis e eletrodomésticos do local. "Fui erguer tudo, móvel, geladeira, fica tudo lá dentro. Fazia tempo que não ocorria isso de novo. Enchia, mas não assim. Dessa vez foi bem forte. Assusta", contou.

Extravasamento do Rio Piracicaba na altura da 'Rua do Porto', Avenida Beira Rio

Não atravesse áreas alagadas nem enxurradas;

Mantenha distância de árvores, postes e fios elétricos;

Em situações de risco, procure um local seguro.

No balanço parcial do mês, Piracicaba registrou 232,7 milímetros (mm) de chuvas entre os dias 1º e 24 de outubro.

A marca supera a média histórica de precipitação em mais que o dobro da expectativa para o período, que é de 110 milímetros, segundo dados do Posto Meteorológico Jesus Marden do Santos da Escola Superior de Agricultura “Luiz de Queiroz”.

Segundo a Prefeitura de Piracicaba, os pontos mencionados na reportagem são locais de recorrentes alagamentos quando ocorrem fortes pancadas de chuvas.

Avenida Jaime Pereira (Estrada do Bongue) interditada neste domingo (25) — Foto: Edijan Del Santo/EPTV

O Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet) emitiu alertas amarelo e laranja de perigo tempestades nas 18 cidades da área de cobertura do g1 Piracicaba e região entre este domingo e segunda-feira (26).

O aviso aponta risco de chuvas de 60 mm/hora ou 50 e 100 mm/dia, ventos intensos (60-100 km/h), e queda de granizo, bem como de corte de energia elétrica, estragos em plantações, queda de árvores e de alagamentos.

não se abrigue debaixo de árvores, pois há risco de queda e descargas elétricas e não estacione veículos próximos a torres de transmissão e placas de propaganda

Se possível, desligue aparelhos elétricos e quadro geral de energia.

Obtenha mais informações junto à Defesa Civil (telefone 199) e ao Corpo de Bombeiros (telefone 193)

Rua Luiz de Queiroz em Piracicaba tem trechos de alagamentos — Foto: Gustavo Nolasco/ EPTV

O Rio Corumbataí também transbordou neste domingo, com pontos de atenção voltados para bairros como Santa Terezinha, Vila Rios e IAA-Bessy.

articles.title: Homem é encontrado morto a facadas e atropelado em rua em Campo Grande | G1
articles.standfirst: Odair de Souza, de 57 anos, foi encontrado morto na manhã desta segunda-feira (26), no bairro Danúbio Azul. Polícia investiga se ele foi levado ao local ou já estava na região.
articles.summary: Odair de Souza, de 57 anos, foi encontrado morto na manhã desta segunda-feira (26), no bairro Danúbio Azul. Polícia investiga se ele foi levado ao local ou já estava na região.
articles.body:
Homem é morto a facadas e atropelado em rua de Campo Grande — Foto: Gabi Cenciarelli, g1 MS

Um homem identificado como Odair de Souza, de 57 anos, foi encontrado morto a facadas e atropelado na manhã desta segunda-feira (26), na Rua Lise Rose, no bairro Danúbio Azul, na saída para Cuiabá, em Campo Grande .

Segundo a titular da 3ª Delegacia de Polícia de Campo Grande, Sueli Araújo Lima Rocha, os levantamentos preliminares indicam que a vítima recebeu diversos golpes de faca no tórax. Também foram encontradas lesões nos braços que podem indicar uma tentativa de defesa.

Após as agressões, um veículo passou por cima do homem. A polícia trabalha inicialmente com a hipótese de que o homicídio tenha sido cometido por mais de uma pessoa.

De acordo com a delegada, havia sinais de sangue no chão, o que indica que as agressões podem ter ocorrido na própria rua onde o corpo foi encontrado.

Polícia investiga circunstâncias do crime

A investigação vai apurar se Odair foi levado até o local ou se já estava na região antes de ser morto.

Durante a perícia, foi encontrado um pequeno cachimbo no bolso da vítima. O objeto será considerado na apuração, mas ainda não há confirmação de que o homem fosse usuário de drogas.

Odair era morador do Jardim Tijuca e, conforme o levantamento preliminar da polícia, não tinha passagens policiais.

O caso será encaminhado à Delegacia Especializada de Homicídios e Proteção à Pessoa (DHPP), responsável pela investigação.

articles.title: Urnas substituídas na Paraíba: 50 máquinas trocadas no 2º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Número de substituições diminuiu em relação ao 1º turno. Em duas cidades, urnas tiverem teclas coladas.
articles.summary: O total de urnas substituídas na Paraíba caiu para 50 no 2º turno, apesar de casos de vandalismo com teclas coladas em cidades do Agreste.
articles.body:
Urna eletrônica eleições mulher — Foto: Tribunal Superior Eleitoral/TSE

O 2º turno de votação das Eleições Gerais de 2026 ocorreu neste domingo (25) e, durante o pleito, 50 urnas foram substituídas na Paraíba. O número caiu em relação ao 1º turno, que totalizou a substituição de 67 equipamentos.

De acordo com o Tribunal Regional Eleitoral da Paraíba (TRE-PB), no 2º turno, foram registradas duas ocorrências graves de violação de urnas nos municípios de Puxinanã e Campina Grande , ambos no Agreste do estado. Nos dois casos, os equipamentos foram substituídos após a identificação de teclas coladas.

O número de urnas substituídas no 2º turno representa 0,47% do total de equipamentos utilizados no estado. A maioria das substituições ocorre no município de João Pessoa , um dos maiores colégios eleitorais do estado.

A causa das substituições ainda não foi divulgada.

Segundo a assessoria do TRE-PB, na capital, as urnas que apresentaram problemas já estavam no radar do órgão por serem mais antigas. Os equipamentos de 2013 foram colocados na região de João Pessoa para que a troca fosse realizada de forma mais rápida caso algum problema ocorresse.

articles.title: Imprensa mundial destaca reeleição de Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente Lula (PT) derrotou o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e se tornou o primeiro presidente da história do Brasil a ser eleito quatro vezes pelo voto popular.
articles.summary: Presidente Lula (PT) derrotou o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e se tornou o primeiro presidente da história do Brasil a ser eleito quatro vezes pelo voto popular.
articles.body:
A imprensa mundial deu amplo destaque à reeleição do presidente Lula (PT) nesta segunda-feira (26), no dia seguinte ao pleito. Os jornais destacaram o aspecto surpreendente da virada inédita e projetam o panorama para seu novo governo.

Lula derrotou o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) na votação no domingo, o que marcou a primeira vez na história em que um candidato é eleito após ter ficado em 2º lugar no primeiro turno. O presidente obteve 51,79% dos votos válidos, enquanto Flávio ficou com 48,21%.

O New York Times , dos Estados Unidos, destacou o poder de Lula para a virada: "O líder político mais influente da América Latina freia avanço da direita";

O Le Monde , da França, afirmou que o resultado foi uma "surpresa para todos";

O La Nación , da Argentina, falou em "reviravolta no Brasil" e "virada inédita";

A BBC , do Reino Unido, também destacou a "vitória surpreendente" de Lula;

A CNN Internacional , dos Estados Unidos, afirmou que "o Brasil se mantém à esquerda enquanto a América Latina vira à direita";

O The Telegraph , do Reino Unido, afirmou que a "guerra no Brasil continua", em referência à polarização que permanece no país e o Congresso brasileiro avesso ao petista.

Reeleição do presidente Lula destacada na página inicial do jornal The New York Times, dos Estados Unidos, em 26 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução/The New York Times

O jornal norte-americano "The New York Times" destacou no topo de sua página inicial a reeleição de Lula e o panorama do resultado da eleição brasileira.

Em reportagem, o jornal deu evidência ao poder de Lula para a virada: "O líder político mais influente da América Latina freou o avanço da direita".

O jornal afirmou que Lula alcançou uma "recuperação memorável e espetacular", além de destacar o tamanho da vitória do presidente brasileiro frente à pressão exercida pelo governo Trump.

"A improvável vitória de Lula no Brasil representou uma impressionante rejeição ao avanço da direita, dando novo fôlego a um movimento de esquerda que parecia à beira da extinção na América Latina. (...) Lula ofereceu um exemplo raro de resistência à estratégia de Washington de projetar seu poderio militar e econômico na região, enfrentando Trump enquanto o presidente americano tentava pressionar o Brasil com tarifas e sanções", escreveu.

Reportagem do jornal Le Monde, da França, sobre a reeleição de Lula em 26 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução/Le Monde

O francês "Le Monde" afirmou que a reeleição de Lula ocorreu "para surpresa de todos", porque as pesquisas eleitorais indicavam Flávio Bolsonaro à frente apesar de projetarem cenários de empate técnico.

"O presidente brasileiro de esquerda, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, foi reeleito neste domingo, conquistando, contra todas as expectativas, um quarto mandato inédito, mas seu rival conservador, Flávio Bolsonaro, anunciou a intenção de pedir a anulação do pleito", afirmou a reportagem.

Em artigo de opinião, o "Le Monde" também afirmou que "a extrema direita foi derrotada no Brasil" , em referência ao bolsonarismo, e destacou que Lula terá uma tarefa difícil para reduzir a desigualdade e defender as instituições brasileiras" diante de um Congresso dominado pela extrema direita".

Reeleição do presidente Lula destacada na página inicial do jornal La Nación, da Argentina, em 26 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução/La Nación

O jornal argentino "La Nación" também destacou a reeleição de Lula no topo de sua página inicial e falou que o pleito representou uma "reviravolta no Brasil". Também destacou que Lula obteve uma "virada inédita".

O veículo também mencionou a polêmica com denúncias de ambos os partidos e com a extensão de votação e destacou que Flávio Bolsonaro vai pedir a anulação dos resultados.

Reeleição do presidente Lula destacada na página inicial da rede britânica BBC em 26 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução/BBC

A rede britânica BBC também destacou no topo de sua página inicial a reeleição de Lula e falou em "vitória surpreendente" do petista.

"A eleição foi marcada por uma disputa acirrada e contraria uma tendência regional mais ampla de ascensão de líderes de direita, escreve nosso editor para a América Latina", escreveu.

O veículo também afirmou que Lula enfrentará um Congresso "hostil" e um país dividido.

Reeleição do presidente Lula destacada na página inicial da TV CNN Internacional, dos Estados Unidos, em 26 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução/CNN Internacional

A TV CNN Internacional afirmou que "o Brasil se mantém à esquerda enquanto a América Latina vira à direita".

Reportagem do tablóide The Telegraph, do Reino Unido, sobre a reeleição de Lula em 26 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução/The Telegraph

O tablóide britânico "The Telegraph" afirmou que "Lula ganhou, mas a guerra continua para o Brasil", em referência à polarização que permanece no país e o Congresso brasileiro avesso ao petista.

articles.title: Porcelanato retificado: o que significa e por que importa no projeto | G1
articles.standfirst: Bordas precisas, rejunte fino e variação de tonalidade: três detalhes que valem conferir antes de fechar o piso.
articles.summary: Bordas precisas, rejunte fino e variação de tonalidade: três detalhes que valem conferir antes de fechar o piso.
articles.body:
Retificado é o porcelanato que passa por um corte nas bordas depois da queima, para que todas as peças fiquem com as mesmas medidas. Esse acabamento deixa as laterais retas e as dimensões mais precisas do que em peças não retificadas, que têm bordas levemente arredondadas.

Com as bordas precisas, as peças podem ser assentadas com juntas estreitas, o que dá ao piso um aspecto mais contínuo, especialmente em formatos grandes. A Biancogres tem porcelanatos retificados em diferentes formatos e acabamentos entre os produtos disponíveis na Panorama, como 60x120, 90x90 e peças que imitam madeira.

Tonalidade: a informação que fica na embalagem

Mesmo dentro de um mesmo modelo, pode haver variação de tonalidade entre as peças, e é isso que o fabricante indica na caixa. Vale conferir essa informação antes de comprar e, de preferência, abrir mais de uma caixa e misturar as peças durante o assentamento, para que o resultado fique bem distribuído no ambiente.

Peças maiores deixam qualquer desnível do contrapiso mais evidente. Por isso, o nivelamento da base e a escolha da argamassa adequada ao tamanho e ao peso da peça fazem parte do planejamento, junto com o uso de espaçadores e niveladores durante a aplicação.

Ao dimensionar a quantidade, é comum considerar uma margem para cortes e perdas, que costuma ser maior em formatos grandes ou assentamentos diagonais. Guardar uma caixa extra do mesmo lote também facilita eventuais reparos no futuro.

articles.title: Prefeitura na BA é punida após expor dados médicos de 1,2 mil pessoas | G1
articles.standfirst: Vazamento ocorreu em setembro de 2025 na lista de suspensão do passe livre no Diário Oficial do Município de Feira de Santana. Documento expôs diagnósticos de HIV, anemia falciforme e fibromialgia.
articles.summary: Vazamento ocorreu em setembro de 2025 na lista de suspensão do passe livre no Diário Oficial do Município. Documento expôs diagnósticos de HIV, anemia falciforme e fibromialgia.
articles.body:
Centro de Feira de Santana — Foto: Prefeitura Municipal de Feira de Santana

A Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) puniu a Prefeitura de Feira de Santana , segunda maior cidade da Bahia, após a divulgação de dados médicos de 1.241 pessoas no Diário Oficial do Município, em setembro de 2025. Segundo a ANPD, a gestão recebeu uma advertência e terá que publicar um aviso sobre a infração no site oficial por seis meses , além de adotar medidas para evitar novos vazamentos.

O vazamento aconteceu em 20 de setembro de 2025, quando a prefeitura publicou uma lista com os nomes de pessoas que teriam o benefício do passe livre no transporte coletivo suspenso por determinação judicial. Além dos nomes, o documento expôs informações sobre a saúde dos beneficiários, incluindo diagnósticos de HIV, anemia falciforme e fibromialgia.

A edição do Diário Oficial ficou disponível ao público por algumas horas e foi retirada do ar no mesmo dia , após a prefeitura identificar o problema. Na época, a Secretaria Municipal de Mobilidade Urbana (Semob) informou que a divulgação ocorreu devido a uma falha no sistema e lamentou o ocorrido.

Após receber uma denúncia sobre o caso, a ANPD iniciou uma investigação para apurar a divulgação dos dados e verificar quais providências foram adotadas para reduzir os possíveis danos às pessoas afetadas.

A agência concluiu que a prefeitura cometeu seis infrações à Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD). Entre as irregularidades identificadas estão o uso de informações sem finalidade legítima, a exposição pública de dados que deveriam ser protegidos e a falta de medidas de segurança adequadas para evitar o vazamento.

A ANPD também constatou que o município não comunicou o incidente à própria agência nem às pessoas afetadas, embora a legislação exija essa comunicação em situações que possam provocar riscos ou danos relevantes aos titulares dos dados.

Outro problema apontado foi a falta de resposta da prefeitura a uma solicitação formal de informações feita durante a fiscalização. Segundo a agência, a omissão dificultou o trabalho de apuração.

Prefeitura terá que adotar medidas de proteção

Prefeitura publicou lista com nomes de pessoas que vivem com HIV ao suspender benefício — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Além da advertência e da obrigação de divulgar a infração na primeira página do site institucional durante seis meses, a prefeitura deverá implementar medidas para evitar novos vazamentos.

Nomear um responsável pela proteção de dados pessoais;

Elaborar e divulgar políticas de privacidade e de segurança da informação;

Criar um plano de resposta a incidentes de segurança;

Estabelecer regras para o compartilhamento de dados entre secretarias municipais;

Adotar uma etapa de análise prévia para verificar os riscos à privacidade antes da publicação de informações no Diário Oficial;

Apresentar um plano de capacitação para servidores que trabalham com dados pessoais;

Eliminar informações tratadas sem base legal ou finalidade válida;

Disponibilizar, no site da prefeitura, informações claras sobre os dados coletados, as finalidades do tratamento, os compartilhamentos realizados e os direitos dos cidadãos.

A agência informou que órgãos públicos não estão sujeitos à aplicação de multas administrativas previstas na LGPD. Por isso, as sanções aplicadas à prefeitura incluem advertência e publicização da infração, além das medidas corretivas.

Por que os dados divulgados são sensíveis?

Informações sobre a saúde de uma pessoa são classificadas como dados pessoais sensíveis pela LGPD. Isso significa que elas exigem cuidados específicos para evitar exposição indevida, discriminação e outros prejuízos aos titulares.

No caso de pessoas que vivem com HIV, a divulgação de nomes associados ao diagnóstico pode expor os pacientes a situações de constrangimento e estigmatização . O tratamento adequado permite que essas pessoas tenham uma rotina ativa e saudável, e o diagnóstico não deve ser motivo de discriminação.

A legislação brasileira protege a intimidade, a vida privada e os dados pessoais. Por isso, mesmo quando uma publicação oficial é necessária para cumprir uma determinação judicial, as informações divulgadas precisam se limitar ao que é necessário para atender à finalidade do ato.

A lista foi publicada quando a prefeitura informou a suspensão do benefício de passe livre no transporte coletivo urbano , em cumprimento a uma decisão judicial que revogou uma tutela provisória de urgência concedida anteriormente.

A portaria determinava que os beneficiários devolvessem os cartões no prazo de cinco dias úteis e apresentassem defesa por escrito ou documentos à Secretaria Municipal de Mobilidade Urbana. O procedimento poderia resultar na suspensão ou no cancelamento definitivo do benefício.

Na época, a Semob afirmou que a divulgação dos nomes ocorreu por uma falha no sistema e reforçou o compromisso da administração municipal com a privacidade e a dignidade das pessoas. A prefeitura informou que abriu uma sindicância interna para investigar o caso.

Os processos de fiscalização e de aplicação das sanções estão disponíveis para consulta no Sistema Eletrônico de Informações da ANPD.

Em nota, a Procuradoria-Geral de Feira de Santana informou que aguarda o recebimento da notificação oficial referente à recomendação da Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD). Após o recebimento e a análise do documento, serão adotadas as providências cabíveis.

articles.title: 'Gyanesh Kumar must quit': Kharge lists INDIA bloc's three key demands amid SIR row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Monday outlined three key demands of the INDIA bloc over alleged irregularities in voter rolls,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Monday outlined three key demands of the INDIA bloc over alleged irregularities in voter rolls, calling for Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, an immediate halt to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and a return to paper ballots.In a post on X, Kharge accused the Narendra Modi government of protecting Kumar despite what he described as repeated revelations of “vote theft”. He also alleged collusion between the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Election Commission of India (ECI).Kharge urged citizens to join the INDIA bloc’s ‘Save Votes–Save the Nation’ march and mega rally at Delhi’s Ramlila Maidan on November 1.Kharge flags voter roll irregularitiesRaising questions over the transparency of the SIR process, Kharge said the Election Commission had refused to disclose information about the software used in the exercise in response to a Right to Information (RTI) request, citing “Trade Secrets”.He also claimed that details of 16.18 lakh Form-6 applications in Uttar Pradesh had not been made public. Form 6 is used to apply for inclusion in the electoral roll.Referring to Pilibhit, Kharge alleged that irregularities had been detected in records relating to 10,470 voters. He said authorities had subsequently been compelled to order an investigation into Forms 6, 7 and 8 across Uttar Pradesh. These forms are used for voter registration, objections or deletions, and corrections or changes to electoral roll entries, respectively.“Even after countless revelations of vote theft, the Modi government is resorting to every possible trick to protect Gyanesh Kumar!” Kharge said in his post.Three demands of INDIA blocOutlining the opposition alliance’s demands, Kharge called for Kumar’s resignation and the repeal of the 2023 law that provides legal protection to the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners in certain circumstances.He also demanded an immediate suspension of the SIR exercise and the restoration of names of voters allegedly removed illegally from electoral rolls.The third demand was that all elections be conducted using paper ballots instead of electronic voting machines.“This is not just a fight to save votes; it is a people's struggle to save the Constitution and democracy,” Kharge said.Calling on citizens to participate in the November 1 mobilisation, he urged them to gather at Ramlila Maidan in the national capital for the ‘Save Votes–Save the Nation’ march and rally.“I appeal to every conscious citizen of the country -Come to Delhi on November 1! articles.title: Ebola outbreak: DR Congo nurse killed in attack as Uganda tightens border
articles.summary: Local youths reportedly accused the health workers of contaminating water sources and spreading Ebola.
articles.body:
A nurse has been killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack as they were responding to an Ebola alert in north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

The two were targeted by local youths who accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the Ebola virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi. The World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the attack.

In an attempt to prevent the virus spreading, neighbouring Uganda has banned all non-essential travel to and from DR Congo and says its citizens returning from there will be quarantined for 21 days.

More than 4,800 people have died and nearly 10,000 been infected in DR Congo since this outbreak began in May.

Reacting to the attack in DR Congo, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said health workers "must be able to carry out their duties in safety and dignity", adding that healthcare personnel should always be protected.

The UN agency also extended its condolences to the family and colleagues of the nurse who was killed and wished the injured worker a swift recovery.

The BBC has contacted the Ebola response team for comment on the circumstances surrounding the attack in DR Congo.

This is not the first time such an attack has happened in DR Congo. Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents during the first 100 days after the outbreak was declared.

Earlier this month, two countries - Kenya and Nigeria - reported their first cases of Ebola linked to the current outbreak.

The patient in Nigeria was on Monday flown from Abuja to Switzerland for further treatment.

She is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya. She was evacuated alongside her husband, who has shown no symptoms.

Nigeria's health ministry said she was stable, conscious and able to communicate.

Authorities are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus.

The new restrictions announced in Uganda come after questions were raised over her case and that of a Kenyan businessman. Both tested positive for Ebola after travelling through Uganda, even though no cases have been reported there since August.

The Kenyan had arrived from DR Congo where he had business interests.

Only essential travellers, including aid workers, truck drivers and security personnel, will be allowed to cross the border from DR Congo to Uganda, subject to strict health screening, the health ministry announced.

In addition, all travellers entering Uganda, regardless of their country of origin, will be required to complete locator forms to facilitate contact tracing where necessary.

It said returning Ugandans would "undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost".

About 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan patient have all been discharged, it added.

In Kenya , the first group of 20 contacts of the first case have gone home, after spending 21 days in quarantine, the health ministry announced on Monday.

Another 98 are still being supervised, while seven people who have tested positive for Ebola were stable it said.

The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi. A second woman, related to the businessman, died over the weekend.

'They said it isn't real': Ebola rumours fuel attacks on health workers

Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected

"All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola," Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC's Newsday programme.

Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country free of the disease in August.

The two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day.

Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients.

Ugandan officials had previously said the patient in Nigeria had travelled to eastern DR Congo, only transiting through Uganda. On Sunday, however, the health ministry said Uganda and Nigeria were both working to establish her movements, complete travel history and possible routes of exposure.

The Ugandan health minister said the recent cases meant the risk had not ended and further underscored the need to "remain vigilant".

"We share a border with [DR Congo], where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties," Baryomunsi said.

The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind this outbreak is relatively rare and there is still no vaccine or specific treatment - though trials are under way.
