articles.title: Storm Boelo clean-up begins as thousands left without power
articles.summary: Around 90,000 properties are without power after Scotland and north England is battered by strong winds.
articles.body:
A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.

The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 90,000 properties are still without power as of Monday.

Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old in Mid Kelton, Dumfries and Galloway.

The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for strong winds from 18:00 on Monday to 03:00 on Tuesday across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland.

The Met Office has warned that further power cuts in areas covered by the warning are likely and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.

Coastal communities could also be affected by spray or large waves, while travel delays are expected.

Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.

Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.

"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," Slade told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.

Storm Boelo clears but more wind and rain bears down on UK

Marcus Reed, the operations director at a home fragrance manufacturer, said his factory and shop in Lyndal, Cumbria would be without power until Tuesday evening.

He told the Today programme that he has had to turn away employees and customers.

"To lose two days manufacturing and distribution is going to be really disruptive," he said, adding that it was bad timing as it was "the busiest time of the year" for his business in the lead-up to Christmas.

"This is probably the worst situation I've experienced in my time here; we've had ad hoc issues over weekends where we've lost power, but it's been contained within a 12-hour period. It's the first time anything like this has happened, it's very serious."

Wendy McKinney, whose bathroom shop in the seaside town of Largs in North Ayrshire was flooded on Sunday, told the Today programme the storm had been "devastating to local businesses".

She said the local council only handed out sandbags after flooding had already started:"[They] were just left in the middle of the street yesterday afternoon on pallets just for everybody just to try and help themselves, but it was too little too late."

North Ayrshire Council told the BBC that it had distributed almost 300 sandbags in Largs and Saltcoats and would continue to "respond where it has been safe and appropriate to do so".

A spokesperson said council teams "followed established resilience procedures" but would review flooding reports and "consider any lessons that can be learned".

Disruption to travel has continued on Monday, and some schools in Scotland have been shut either due to lack of power, heating, water or damage.

Another yellow warning of wind has been issued by the Met Office, covering much of Scotland, as well as parts of northern England and Northern Ireland from 03:00 to 23:59 on Tuesday.

Monday morning has seen rain in many parts of south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and this is moving north-eastwards reaching central, eastern and northern England, as well as most of Scotland, by around lunchtime.

Winds will also strengthen throughout Monday, and it will turn even windier overnight as the area of low pressure passes close to Northern Ireland and north-west Scotland with gusts peaking on Tuesday.

articles.title: A cat vanished after her family's car crashed in 2020; six years later, one tiny microchip brought her home
articles.summary: A cat named Pandora has been reunited with her family six years after disappearing during a serious road accident in Scotland.
articles.body: A cat named Pandora has been reunited with her family six years after disappearing during a serious road accident in Scotland. In 2020, Pandora was travelling with her owners, Mary and Billy Bowie, who were moving from Colchester, England, to Fraserburgh, Aberdeenshire, when their van crashed near the village of Errol in Perthshire. The vehicle rolled several times, throwing Pandora's cat basket out of the van and leaving the frightened animal missing. Despite returning to the area and appealing for help, the family could not find her. The mystery remained unresolved until August 2026, when a Cats Protection volunteer scanned a microchip belonging to a cat found near Perth and discovered the information that would lead Pandora back to her owners.A road accident that separated Pandora from her familyPandora and her sister, Ziggy, had been adopted by the Bowies as kittens from the RSPCA in 2017. When the family began moving from England to Scotland three years later, the cats travelled with them in separate vehicles.Billy was driving a van carrying Pandora, while Mary followed in another car with their daughter, grandson and Ziggy. Near Errol in Perthshire, Billy's van was involved in a serious crash and rolled several times. Pandora's basket was thrown from the vehicle, and the cat disappeared.Mary and Billy searched around the crash site, but Pandora could not be found. Although Billy had escaped serious injury, the family was left distressed by the disappearance of their pet during an already traumatic journey.The family continued searching for their missing catAfter moving to Fraserburgh, the Bowies did not give up on finding Pandora. They returned to the area where the accident had happened, despite the journey taking around two and a half hours from their new home.The family also appealed for information through a local Facebook group. Some people reported seeing a black cat wearing a distinctive blue-and-green collar, which matched Pandora's description. However, nobody managed to catch her, and the sightings did not lead to a reunion.As the months turned into years, the family remained without answers about what had happened to Pandora. Her disappearance had begun with a sudden accident, and there was no clear indication of where she had gone or whether she was still in the area.A microchip scan provides the breakthroughThe breakthrough came in 2026 after a local woman contacted Cats Protection about a cat that repeatedly tried to enter her home. Fiona Morrison, a volunteer with the charity, went to investigate and put down food to help her approach the animal.Morrison suspected the cat might be a stray and decided to scan it for a microchip. The scan revealed identifying information linked to a family in Fraserburgh, prompting the charity to contact the owners.The discovery connected the cat to Pandora's family, six years after she had disappeared near Errol. A routine identification check had provided the crucial information that years of searching had failed to uncover.An unexpected birthday call brings Pandora homeMary received the news on August 9, 2026, while celebrating her birthday with her family. The call from Cats Protection Perth came as a surprise, particularly because the charity was contacting her from an area some distance from where Pandora had gone missing.A few days later, Mary and Billy travelled to collect their cat. After six years apart, Pandora was finally back with the people who had adopted her as a kitten.Mary said Pandora settled back in well and responded to her name. She also remained attached to the couple's grandson, providing a familiar connection despite the long separation.The role of microchips for missing petsPandora's reunion highlights how a microchip can help identify a missing animal long after it disappears. A microchip contains a unique identification number that can be read with a scanner and matched to the owner's registered contact details.Unlike a GPS tracker, a microchip does not show an animal's location. Its value lies in helping vets, animal welfare workers and members of the public connect a found pet with its registered owner.Cats Protection advises pet owners to keep their microchip registration details up to date so they can be contacted if their animal is found. In Pandora's case, the information remained useful six years after the crash, allowing a volunteer to trace her family and bring an extraordinary reunion within reach.You use AI every day. articles.title: A New Jersey developer filed a $300 million lawsuit after a township moved to block AI data centres; the dispute began with plans for two warehouses
articles.summary: A New Jersey property developer has filed a lawsuit seeking more than $300 million in damages after a township reversed its zoning rules to block
articles.body: A New Jersey property developer has filed a lawsuit seeking more than $300 million in damages after a township reversed its zoning rules to block artificial intelligence (AI) data centres, escalating a dispute that began with plans for two warehouses on vacant farmland. Hexa Builders, a Princeton-based development company, sued Monroe Township in Gloucester County in June 2026, accusing local officials of changing land-use rules and obstructing its revised application. The controversy intensified after residents opposed the prospect of a data centre near established residential areas. The township subsequently adopted ordinances removing data centres from the developer's redevelopment site and prohibiting them across the municipality. The lawsuit challenges the legality of those decisions and raises broader questions about local planning powers as demand for AI computing infrastructure grows.How the dispute began with two warehousesHexa Builders had been pursuing development of a property at 3043 Black Horse Pike in Williamstown, part of a roughly 159-acre redevelopment area in Monroe Township. In September 2022, the township adopted a redevelopment plan for the site, which was subsequently amended. An amendment in 2025 permitted data centres and related operations alongside warehouse, storage and distribution facilities.In September 2025, Hexa applied for preliminary approval to construct two warehouses with a combined floor area of approximately 1.6 million square feet. The township's planning board granted preliminary site-plan approval in January 2026, following a contentious public meeting.Some residents questioned whether the warehouse proposal could eventually lead to a data centre. Their concerns grew as the township's redevelopment plan allowed that type of facility, prompting objections at public meetings.The developer proposed a data centreIn April 2026, Hexa submitted an amended application proposing a data centre of approximately one million square feet in place of the larger warehouse, while retaining a warehouse as part of the development. The company's lawyer said the change followed market interest that had emerged before the township adopted the 2025 amendment allowing data centres.The revised proposal became a focal point of the debate as residents raised concerns about the potential effects of large computing facilities on their community. Data centres can require substantial electricity and cooling infrastructure, while their environmental footprint depends on factors including cooling technology, energy supply and facility design.On April 22, the township council adopted two ordinances restricting data centres. One removed them as a permitted use within Hexa's redevelopment plan, while the other prohibited data centres across Monroe Township. The official redevelopment ordinance cited the site's proximity to established residential areas and the need to ensure that permitted uses remained compatible with their surroundings.Why the planning board rejected the revised applicationOn May 12, 2026, the planning board deemed Hexa's amended application incomplete. The decision became central to the subsequent lawsuit.Hexa alleges that local officials applied submission requirements differently from those used for its warehouse proposal and deliberately prevented the revised application from being deemed complete before the new restrictions took effect. The company also argues that officials responded to public opposition rather than following a consistent land-use approval process. These claims form part of the developer's complaint and have not been established as judicial findings.What Hexa Builders is seeking in courtHexa filed its lawsuit on June 5, 2026, initially in New Jersey Superior Court. The case was transferred to federal court in Camden on July 6. The complaint contains 20 counts and alleges violations of New Jersey's Municipal Land Use Law, the township's application procedures and constitutional protections, including equal protection and freedom of speech.The developer is asking the court to overturn the ordinances, declare its data-centre application complete and award more than $300 million in damages. Hexa's lawyer has described the amount as reflecting the lost value of the proposed project.The damages figure represents the amount sought by the company, not an award made by a court. The legal proceedings will determine whether the developer's claims have merit and whether the township acted unlawfully.The township's positionMonroe Township has defended its authority to amend its zoning rules and has challenged the developer's constitutional arguments. In filings reported in August, the township argued that the fact that data centres support electronic communications does not automatically make a zoning restriction a violation of free-speech protections. Its lawyers also questioned whether Hexa had a contract guaranteeing permission to build a data centre.The township's official ordinance framed the restrictions around the compatibility of development with nearby residential uses and the municipality's redevelopment objectives. The dispute therefore centres on whether officials lawfully exercised their planning powers, rather than simply on whether residents supported or opposed the project.A wider conflict over AI infrastructureThe Monroe Township case is part of a broader backlash against data-centre development in the United States. As technology companies and developers seek more capacity for AI computing, communities have raised concerns about electricity demand, water use, noise and the effects of industrial-scale facilities on residential areas.New Jersey has seen similar legal challenges. Developers also challenged data-centre restrictions in Montgomery and Andover townships, arguing that local officials had blocked proposed projects after initially allowing or considering the relevant uses.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2018, a company sought to mine gravel on 27 acres in Alaska, but neighbours warned the bowl-shaped land would amplify noise; after years of hearings, the state Supreme Court upheld the decision blocking the mine
articles.summary: A gravel mine can change more than a landscape, particularly when nearby homes are exposed to noise and visual disturbance.
articles.body: A gravel mine can change more than a landscape, particularly when nearby homes are exposed to noise and visual disturbance. In Alaska, a dispute over a proposed mine on 27 acres of rural land continued through years of public hearings, appeals and court proceedings. On October 23, 2026, the Alaska Supreme Court upheld the decision denying the mining permit, finding that the local planning commission had the authority to reject the proposal if its impacts could not be adequately reduced. According to the court’s opinion in Beachcomber, LLC v. Kenai Peninsula Borough Planning Commission, available on Justia, the property’s unusual bowl-shaped terrain was central to the dispute.A gravel mine proposed for rural AlaskaBeachcomber LLC, which owned a 41.72-acre property in Anchor Point, applied in 2018 for a conditional land use permit to operate a gravel pit on roughly 27 acres. Under the Kenai Peninsula Borough’s rules, certain excavation projects in rural areas require approval from the borough’s planning commission.The application attracted strong opposition from nearby residents. During a public hearing in July 2018, nearly 30 community members spoke against the proposal, while written comments and petitions raised concerns about noise, dust and visual impacts. The commission voted 6-3 to reject the application, finding that the site’s unusual terrain would make it difficult to reduce the effects on neighbouring properties.Why the land’s shape became centralThe proposed mine was located in a natural depression described by officials and residents as resembling an amphitheatre. The shape of the land was important because it could allow sound to travel towards nearby homes, while conventional barriers might not adequately block noise or views of the excavation. The borough’s rules allowed the commission to require measures such as retaining natural vegetation and constructing earthen berms to reduce noise and visual disturbance. However, commissioners concluded that these measures would not be enough for this particular site.Beachcomber challenged the rejection, arguing that the rules did not give the commission discretion to deny a permit if the applicant met the conditions specified in the code. The dispute then moved through several levels of administrative and judicial review.Years of appeals over the permitAfter the initial rejection, a borough hearing officer agreed with Beachcomber’s interpretation of the rules and sent the application back for reconsideration. In June 2019, the commission approved the permit after applying that interpretation. Neighbour Hans Bilben and other residents appealed the approval. In September 2021, the Alaska Superior Court reversed the decision, ruling that the commission could deny an application if the available conditions could not adequately minimise its impacts.The commission reconsidered the proposal and rejected it again in March 2022, voting 5-2 against the permit. It found that the site’s topography would prevent the permitted barriers from adequately reducing noise and visual effects. A hearing officer upheld that decision, and the Superior Court affirmed it in April 2024. Beachcomber then appealed to the Alaska Supreme Court, challenging the interpretation of the borough code as well as the process used to deny the application.Supreme Court upholds the rejectionIn its October 23, 2026 decision, the Alaska Supreme Court upheld the commission’s denial and the lower courts’ rulings. The justices concluded that the borough code allowed the commission to reject a permit when substantial evidence showed that the available conditions would not adequately minimise noise and visual impacts.The court also rejected Beachcomber’s arguments that the commission had improperly considered public testimony and LiDAR images, which provide detailed information about ground elevation. It explained that community opposition alone could not justify denying a permit, but found that residents’ testimony and visual evidence were relevant to assessing the proposed mine’s effects on neighbouring properties. The decision did not establish a blanket ban on gravel mining in the area. Instead, it confirmed that local authorities could refuse a particular project when the evidence showed that its impacts could not be adequately controlled under the applicable rules.For the residents around the proposed site, the ruling ends this stage of a dispute that began with a permit application in 2018. For Beachcomber, it leaves the mine proposal rejected under the rules applied in the case. The decision also clarifies that meeting specified permit conditions does not automatically guarantee approval when a planning commission has evidence that significant effects on neighbouring properties would remain.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kentucky orchestra has secured $3.2 million to continue its statewide music tour through 2028 after reaching more than 59,000 people across 55 counties
articles.summary: The Louisville Orchestra has received another $3.2 million from the Kentucky General Assembly to continue its statewide In Harmony Tour through 2028.
articles.body: The Louisville Orchestra has received another $3.2 million from the Kentucky General Assembly to continue its statewide In Harmony Tour through 2028. According to the orchestra’s July 2026 impact figures, the programme has reached more than 59,000 people across 55 Kentucky counties through 243 events since launching in November 2022. The initiative combines full-orchestra concerts with educational programmes and community partnerships, bringing live performances to schools, libraries, public spaces and other local venues. The latest allocation brings the General Assembly’s total investment in the In Harmony Tour to $11.8 million, according to the orchestra. The programme’s next announced stops include 3 free concerts in western Kentucky in February 2027.Orchestra reports more than 59,000 people reachedIn its July 22, 2026, announcement, the Louisville Orchestra reported that the In Harmony Tour had reached more than 59,000 people in 55 counties through 243 events. The figures are the orchestra’s reported programme totals as of that announcement, rather than a separately verified count of all activity through the present date. The orchestra’s breakdown includes 47 full-orchestra concerts in 28 counties, which it says reached more than 39,000 audience members. A further 196 community partnership events across 66 unique ZIP codes served more than 20,000 additional participants.The community programme extends beyond traditional concert performances. According to the orchestra, activities can include classroom visits, interactive performances for students, Once Upon an Orchestra programmes at local libraries, small-ensemble concerts and collaborations with local artists, businesses and community organisations. The orchestra says these partnerships are tailored to the needs and character of individual communities. The programme is designed to bring musical performances and educational opportunities to people who may not regularly attend concerts in conventional venues.$11.8 million in legislative supportThe latest $3.2 million allocation will support the In Harmony Tour through 2028. The orchestra said the new funding brings the Kentucky General Assembly’s total investment in the programme to $11.8 million, making the state legislature the largest single funder in the orchestra’s history. The April 2026 funding announcement described the additional allocation as part of Kentucky’s support for the statewide initiative. It also noted that the General Assembly had allocated funding to other cultural organisations in Louisville, including the Kentucky Center for the Arts, Louisville Ballet, Speed Art Museum, the Kentucky Center for African American Heritage and the Frazier History Museum.The $11.8 million figure refers specifically to legislative support for the In Harmony Tour, not to total state spending on arts and culture. The tour is made possible through a partnership with the Kentucky General Assembly and the Tourism, Arts, and Heritage Cabinet. The orchestra also lists additional support from Humana, the Brown-Forman Foundation, Robert W. Rounsavall III and Mary Rounsavall, the Dr. M. Lee Pearce Foundation, and anonymous donors.The tour has featured guest artists and new musicThe orchestra’s April 2026 announcement said previous tour performances had featured artists including Sam Bush, Michael Cleveland and Flamekeeper, Tessa Lark, Ben Sollee and Chris Thile. The programme has also included 7 world premieres by composers from the Louisville Orchestra Creators Corps, according to the orchestra. The tour has taken performances beyond concert halls to locations such as school gymnasiums, courthouse lawns, libraries and public parks. Its community activities include educational visits and partnerships with local organisations.The orchestra says the initiative is drawing attention from orchestras and cultural leaders across the country as a potentially replicable model for public investment in the arts. That characterisation reflects the orchestra’s own description of the programme. A special engagement featuring cellist Yo-Yo Ma was also announced for 2027 in the orchestra’s April funding release. Further details should be confirmed through subsequent programme announcements.Three free concerts planned for February 2027The orchestra announced 3 further In Harmony Tour concerts for western Kentucky in February 2027. The performances are scheduled to begin at 7:30 p.m. Central Time, with doors opening at 6:30 p.m. Central Time. Each concert is planned as a free, 90-minute programme led by Music Director Teddy Abrams. The orchestra said repertoire and additional details would be announced later. Registration for the February performances was also due to open at a later date, with audiences able to sign up through the orchestra’s In Harmony Tour website to receive updates.The February concerts follow the orchestra’s September 2026 stops in Elizabethtown, Frenchburg and Bardstown, which were announced in July. Through its combination of orchestral performances, education programmes and community partnerships, the In Harmony Tour is intended to bring the Louisville Orchestra into communities across Kentucky beyond its traditional concert venues. The orchestra’s July report provides its latest published breakdown of the programme’s reach, while further updates would be needed to establish totals after the September performances.You use AI every day. articles.title: Consultant doctors in England to strike next month
articles.summary: Senior doctors to stage 48-hour walkout, beginning on 25 November, in dispute over pay and pensions.
articles.body:
Consultant doctors in England are to stage a two-day strike next month in a dispute over pay and working conditions.

The walkout will begin on 25 November at 06:59 GMT, with consultants staffing emergency care only.

This is known as Christmas Day cover and is likely to have a major impact on most routine and elective or planned services.

The announcement comes after talks had been taking place with the government over the past month, following the vote in favour of strike action by British Medical Association members in July.

Consultants – the most senior doctors in hospitals – were given a 3.5% pay increase this year.

But the BMA argues pay has fallen by a quarter over the past 17 years, once inflation is taken into account.

The union also wants a reduction in the standard working week, from 40 to 35 hours, and higher pay for out-of-hours work, alongside changes to pensions, including greater flexibility over when they can be taken.

In a joint statement, BMA consultants committee co-chairs Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta, said they had tried to negotiate with the government in "good faith", but "time-and-time again ministers have kicked the can down the road".

"Unfortunately, that road has now run out, and we have been forced to announce strikes.

"Consultants take their responsibilities incredibly seriously, and striking does not come naturally, but we are hearing loud and clear from the profession that they have had enough."

Average earnings for consultants top £150,000 a year.

Basic pay starts at £113,500, with the most experienced getting £150,500.

But many earn tens of thousands in extra payments and awards.

In the strike ballot, 76% of consultants who took part voted in favour of strike action, with just over half of eligible BMA members taking part.

The government says this represents only around one in five consultants employed by the NHS in England voting for strike action, as nearly half are not BMA members.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government had been in "constructive discussions" with the BMA so it was "disappointing" the strike dates had been announced.

She said taking strike action would be "irresponsible" and "place the health service under even greater pressure".

The strike announcement comes as consultants and other doctors are taking part in strike action during November in Northern Ireland .

Consultants last took strike action in England in 2023. The long-running dispute involving resident doctors in England came to an end earlier this year after more than three years of on-and-off strike action.

articles.title: Brazil election: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic comeback over Bolsonaro
articles.summary: The left-wing incumbent president had lost the first round to right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.
articles.body:
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.

Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since the return to civilian rule in 1985 to win an election after losing the first round of voting.

Lula told celebratory crowds this election is a "loss for negativity, lies", later adding "long live democracy".

Flávio Bolsonaro, who is the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled, which experts say is unlikely.

In an unprecedented move, polls were also extended for two hours on Sunday evening after both candidates made requests for different reasons.

Lula's team had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Senator Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as the reason for their request.

The decision - issued by the Supreme Court just as polling stations were due to close - meant that some had already shut and were not able to re-open.

Supreme Court President Kassio Nunes Marques - appointed by the older Bolsonaro - confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voting extension did not cause issues for the count or the electoral process.

Lula secured 51.79% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.21% - a difference of 4.4 million votes between the two candidates.

The result came as a surprise after Bolsonaro - who has the backing of his father - won the first round of voting on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%.

But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one.

Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the first and second rounds of a presidential election since 1989.

As disconsolate Bolsonaro supporters left the house in Brasília where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in São Paulo to celebrate and address his supporters.

"This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country", the former metal worker said. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people."

Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin told him: "You, for the second time, have saved Brazilian democracy."

Lula wins in Brazil but faces hostile Congress and divided country

Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again

Bolsonaro, who had been poised to give a victory speech, said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable" and "impossible".

But electoral law experts have told BBC Brasil that the chances of the results being annulled are remote.

Fernando Neisser from the Institute of Lawyers of São Paulo (Iasp) said it would be "difficult from a legal standpoint" given that the margin of victory was relatively large, and would depend on the "narrative" his lawyers put forward.

Expert Alberto Rollo said that dates for presidential elections in Brazil are fixed and determined by the constitution, which would add another complication to getting it annulled.

Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.

His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030.

But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump.

Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" - which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard".

Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support.

Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.

While Trump has yet to react, other world leaders have been congratulating Lula on his win.

Ecuador President Daniel Noboa Azin said the region had "common enemies, shared challenges, and much to gain when we work together."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "democracy and multilateralism" had won. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez - also a left-wing leader - called it a "great victory", saying "the comeback of global progressivism has just begun". French President Emmanuel Macron said the two nations should work "in service of a more just world".

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called Lula's victory one for the "global south and progressive forces throughout the world".

Additional reporting by Vinícius de S. Mendes, BBC Brasil

articles.title: Zepto charged Rs 34 above MRP on groceries, offered discounts on inflated prices; consumer court ordered to pay Rs 57,000
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Telangana has held Zepto guilty for charging more than the maximum retail price (MRP) for groceries.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Telangana has held Zepto guilty for charging more than the maximum retail price (MRP) for groceries. The commission directed the company to pay Rs 2,000 as compensation to the customer, Rs 5,000 towards litigation expenses and deposit Rs 50,000 in the commission's consumer legal aid account.Customer flags inflated prices on grocery orderAccording to the commission order, K Shiva Ganesh, a 35-year-old advocate from Uppal in Hyderabad, placed an order for tender jackfruit and MTR 3 Minute Poha on Zepto on September 28, 2023. The total bill was Rs 293, including Rs 288 for the items and Rs 5 in handling charges.The complainant alleged that the prices displayed on Zepto's platform were higher than the MRP, with discounts being applied to the inflated prices. He said the practice was misleading consumers and amounted to an unfair trade practice.Ganesh raised the issue with the company and sought action over the pricing discrepancy. He filed a complaint before the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Ranga Reddy, seeking Rs 5 lakh as compensation for mental agony and violation of his fundamental rights, along with Rs 50,000 towards litigation expenses.The company disputed the allegations, saying it was not the manufacturer of the products and sold goods made by other manufacturers. It relied on its terms of service, which stated that product prices could change and that unintended errors in prices or product information could occur.Zepto told the commission that it corrected the pricing error after the customer brought it to its notice. It also claimed that, as a goodwill gesture, it had offered to refund the entire amount paid for the order, but the complainant refused to accept it and demanded an additional Rs 5,000.Commission's finding on ZeptoThe bench comprising president Chitneni Latha Kumari and member Kathyayani Khandavilli examined the invoice, screenshots of the order and bill, the product received and the conversations between the customer and the company.The commission found that the company had charged more than the MRP and offered a discount on the inflated price. It rejected the company's explanation that the pricing discrepancy was an unintended technical or typographical error.“In this case, there is no dispute that the Opposite Parties Zepto online grocery delivery store sold the product at prices exceeding the Maximum Retail Price (MRP), Ex.A1 evidences the same,” the bench said.It further held that offering discounts on inflated prices amounted to deceptive trade practice.“In our view, the action of collecting more than MRP on the online platform attracts the definition of ‘unfair trade’ practice and as the action of the Opposite Parties lacks the transparency and it defeated trustworthiness of the products on their selling prices of the platform,” it added.The commission also noted that selling essential groceries above the MRP could mislead consumers and that the lack of transparency affected their interests. It considered the time and effort required to pursue legal remedies while deciding the relief.“And, observing the frustrating experience of the complainant, we feel it is just and reasonable to direct the Opposite Parties to pay compensation of Rs.2,000,” the commission added.Final orderThe District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Ranga Reddy, partly allowed the complaint on October 13 and directed the two opposite parties to:Pay Rs 2,000 as compensation to the complainant.Pay Rs 5,000 towards litigation expenses.Deposit Rs 50,000 in the Consumer Legal Aid Account of the Ranga Reddy District Consumer Commission.Discontinue the unfair or restrictive trade practice and not repeat it under Section 39(1)(g) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.The company was directed to comply within 45 days of receiving a copy of the order. The commission passed the order on October 13, 2026.The total monetary amount directed to be paid or deposited is Rs 57,000, comprising Rs 7,000 for the complainant and Rs 50,000 for the commission's consumer legal aid account. The commission did not award the Rs 5 lakh in compensation or Rs 50,000 in litigation expenses sought by the complainant.

articles.summary: US forces in the Middle East are prepared to launch potentially major military operations against Iran within 96 hours of receiving an order from
articles.body: US forces in the Middle East are prepared to launch potentially major military operations against Iran within 96 hours of receiving an order from President Donald Trump, with sufficient military assets now deployed in the region to carry out the attacks, CNN reported, citing two US officials.The preparations come amid growing indications that Washington could resume large-scale combat operations against Tehran, despite uncertainty over Trump's final decision and continuing diplomatic efforts to end the conflict. The potential targets include Iranian energy infrastructure, military installations and nuclear facilities, according to CNN.“It will be a big effort,” one of the officials told CNN, describing the scale of the potential operation. The planned strikes could go beyond the limited attacks on Iranian radars, missile launchers and other military assets that can be quickly rebuilt, which have characterised US operations since Trump halted full combat operations earlier this year.Several current and former US officials familiar with internal military planning believe the question is increasingly when, rather than whether, Trump will authorise renewed military action, CNN reported. Some believe an order could come before the end of the year, although the period after the November 3 US midterm elections is considered more likely.The renewed preparations come as the US and Israel face the prospect of Iranian retaliation if hostilities resume. Recent US intelligence assessments indicate that Tehran and Yemen's Houthi rebels are taking the possibility of fresh attacks seriously, according to sources familiar with the assessments cited by CNN.Iran and the Houthis could respond immediately by targeting American personnel and facilities across the region, with the possibility of attacks extending beyond the Middle East, the sources told Israeli news portal Ynet.An October 23 memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio said US intelligence had found that Iran had substantially increased efforts to target American personnel, with plotting efforts reaching advanced stages in the Middle East and other countries, CNN previously reported.US intelligence officials believe Tehran and the Houthis are unlikely to launch pre-emptive attacks at present but would retaliate if American or Israeli forces strike Iran first.The developments follow Trump's recent remarks suggesting that Washington could resume military operations if negotiations fail.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jordan arrests three men suspected of deadly attack on church
articles.summary: No group has yet said it was behind Friday's shooting attack in the village of Hmoud, which left nine Christians dead.
articles.body:
Jordanian security forces have arrested three armed men suspected of a shooting attack at a church last week that killed nine Christians and injured 34 other people, officials say.

The Public Security Directorate (PSD) said the unnamed "terrorists" were located before dawn inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman.

They refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and wounded all three of them, it added. No security personnel were hurt in the shootout.

No group has yet claimed it was behind Friday's attack by gunmen on a funeral at St George's Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hmoud, which is in Karak governorate.

King Abdullah II praised security forces for chasing the suspects "to the very end".

"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he wrote on X.

"We pray that the martyrs' souls rest in peace and wish the injured a speedy recovery. May God protect and watch over Jordan and its people."

Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said authorities would hold to account anyone involved in the attack and were "examining every factor that leads youth toward extremism".

Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.

Verified CCTV footage from Friday showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church.

A second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes.

One man who was at the church told BBC Arabic that the attack lasted around 15 minutes.

"Some [people at the funeral] were taking cover, some were cradling the dead, others were holding their sons close, some were grabbing their children and fleeing, while others were holding onto their friends who were with them at the church," Khalid al-Mdanat said.

He added that the gunmen fled in a pick-up truck, "firing as they went".

On Sunday, the Greek Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem, Theophilos III, visited wounded survivors of the attack, which he condemned as a "vile, cowardly, and bloody act".

He also led the funeral at St George's of eight of the victims - Dr Maher Zureiqat, Ihab al-Halsa, Dr Fadi al-Halsa, Dr Khaled al-Halsa, Dr Asim al-Burqan, Alaa al-Masarwa, Marwan Khaitan and Mazen al-Qassous - which was attended by thousands of people.

The ninth victim, Dr Mohammed al-Qassous, was laid to rest near Amman on Monday.

articles.title: A Georgia county rejected a 700-acre data-centre campus for the second time in seven months; the proposal covered 4.4 million square feet
articles.summary: A proposed data-centre campus spanning approximately 700 acres in Douglas County, Georgia, was rejected for the second time in seven months after county
articles.body: A proposed data-centre campus spanning approximately 700 acres in Douglas County, Georgia, was rejected for the second time in seven months after county commissioners voted against the development on July 7, 2026. The proposal, submitted by East Village Dothan LLC, an applicant linked to data-centre developer EdgeConneX, called for a campus comprising five buildings with a combined floor area of approximately 4.4 million square feet. Located near Interstate 20 and Liberty Road, outside Villa Rica, the project faced opposition from residents concerned about its potential effects on surrounding neighbourhoods and natural resources. Commissioners voted 4-1 against the rezoning request, preventing the development from proceeding under the proposed plan. The decision followed a recommendation from the county's planning commission to reject the application.Where was the proposed data-centre campus located in GeorgiaThe proposed development was planned for land near the Liberty Road exit on Interstate 20, close to Villa Rica in western Douglas County. The property lies near the county line with Carroll County, west of Atlanta, and includes land near Liberty Road, Suddeth Road and the Clinton Nature Preserve.The proposed site covered approximately 700 acres within Douglas County, with the wider property extending into the neighbouring city of Villa Rica. The applicant sought changes to the county's land-use plan and zoning classification to permit the construction of the data-centre campus and associated infrastructure.The location was significant because the property included largely undeveloped land in an area where residential communities and natural spaces could be affected by large-scale commercial construction.Why was the project rejected?The proposal faced opposition over its compatibility with the county's long-term development plans and the potential effects on local infrastructure and the environment.Douglas County planning officials raised concerns about traffic, public safety, fire protection and water quality. The county's planning and zoning manager, Allison Duncan, said the proposed development was inconsistent with the area's long-term growth plan and questioned whether the location was suitable for such a large data-centre campus.The property's location in the Dog River Basin also drew attention. The basin feeds the county's main drinking-water reservoir, making the protection of water resources an important consideration in evaluating the development.The county's planning and zoning commission recommended rejecting the application before the final vote. On July 7, the Board of Commissioners voted 4-1 against the rezoning request, with District 1 Commissioner Henry Mitchell casting the sole vote against denial.Residents raised concerns about noise, water and electricityThe proposal prompted a heated public debate, with residents expressing concerns about how a large data-centre campus might affect their communities.Noise was one issue raised during the public hearing. Opponents used audio demonstrations to illustrate the potential disturbance associated with data-centre operations. Residents also questioned the project's possible water requirements and the implications of additional electricity demand.Data centres house servers and other computing equipment that require reliable electricity and cooling systems. The scale of the proposed development therefore brought questions about infrastructure capacity and the long-term consequences for the surrounding area.However, the concerns expressed during the hearing were not proof that the project would necessarily cause water shortages or increase household electricity bills. They formed part of the debate over whether the development was appropriate for the site.The revised proposal was smaller than the original planThe development had previously been proposed on a larger scale.An earlier application for the Hickman Property outlined a project comprising 11 data-centre buildings with a combined floor area of approximately 6.22 million square feet. It also included warehouse and distribution space. The original plan covered a wider 736-acre property, of which approximately 700 acres were in Douglas County.The revised proposal reduced the planned data-centre floor area to around 4.4 million square feet and called for a campus comprising five buildings, according to Data Center Dynamics. Other reporting described six buildings.Despite the reduction in the proposed floor area, the development continued to face opposition. The county's planning commission recommended denial, and the Board of Commissioners subsequently rejected the revised application.The developer cited potential economic benefitsThe project also had supporters who argued that it could provide economic benefits to Douglas County.Representatives for the developer said the campus could create between 200 and 300 permanent jobs. Supporters also pointed to the potential for additional county revenue, an important consideration as local officials grapple with infrastructure needs and public spending.During the public debate, Commissioner Mark Alcarez highlighted the county's road infrastructure challenges and the need to identify revenue sources without placing additional pressure on property taxpayers.The disagreement reflected a broader question facing communities considering large data-centre developments: whether the expected employment and tax benefits justify the potential effects on local infrastructure, natural resources and residential areas.What happens to the project now?The July 2026 decision prevented the proposed campus from moving forward under the rejected application. The property remains subject to its existing land-use and zoning designations, and a future attempt to develop the site as a data centre would require the necessary approvals.As of the latest available project-tracking information in October 2026, no new application or appeal had been recorded following the rejection.The decision also came amid wider debate across the Atlanta metropolitan area over data-centre expansion. Douglas County already has substantial data-centre development, including operational buildings, facilities under construction and other proposals under review.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Indiana husband withdrew $220,823 from his retirement account without telling his wife; the divorce court ensured an equal division of marital assets while accounting for unpaid child support
articles.summary: An Indiana divorce case has drawn attention to how courts handle retirement savings withdrawn by one spouse before a marriage formally ends.
articles.body: An Indiana divorce case has drawn attention to how courts handle retirement savings withdrawn by one spouse before a marriage formally ends. Clifford Dale Hunt withdrew $220,823.33 from his retirement account without his wife Valerie Hunt’s knowledge shortly before filing for divorce in 2023. The dispute later reached the Indiana Court of Appeals, where Valerie challenged the division of their marital property and the calculation of unpaid child support. In a decision issued on 23 March 2026, the appellate court upheld the trial court’s ruling on both issues.The Indiana husband’s $220,823 retirement withdrawal affected the divorceAccording to the Indiana Court of Appeals’ decision in Valerie Renee Hunt v. Clifford Dale Hunt, the couple married in 2003 and had 3 children, one of whom had reached adulthood by the time of the proceedings.In April 2023, Clifford moved into an apartment and told Valerie that he intended to file for divorce. Shortly afterwards, he withdrew $220,823.33 from his retirement account without informing her.Clifford filed his divorce petition in October 2023. At that point, the retirement account from which he had withdrawn the money had a balance of $309,412.46.The withdrawal became a central issue when the couple’s assets were assessed for division. Valerie argued that the money should still count as part of the marital estate, even though Clifford had already removed it from the account.The court found the withdrawal was a dissipation of marital assets, meaning the marital wealth had been spent or taken away in a way that should be considered in dividing the couple’s property.The ruling indicated that taking out money before divorce proceedings does not automatically mean the money will be excluded from a court’s consideration of how to divide a couple’s shared assets.Why did the court count the withdrawn retirement money as marital propertyThe Indiana Court of Appeals explained that state law requires marital property to be divided in a just and reasonable manner. Although an equal division is generally presumed to be fair, the court can consider whether one spouse’s conduct makes a different approach appropriate.The court considered Clifford’s withdrawal as part of the wider financial picture rather than treating the money as though it had disappeared from the couple’s assets.According to the decision, the trial court included the $220,823.33 in the marital estate attributed to Clifford when calculating the final distribution. It also found that Valerie had rebutted the usual presumption of an equal division because of his handling of the funds.A separate explanation by Indiana law firm Dixon & Moseley provides context for how retirement accounts are treated in divorces across the state. The firm explains that Indiana follows a ‘one-pot approach’ to marital property. Assets belonging to either spouse are counted in the marital estate under this system, even if some assets were acquired before the marriage. The timing and source of contributions can still influence how a court decides to divide the property.The firm also notes that retirement savings accumulated during a marriage are generally treated as marital property. Individual retirement accounts, or IRAs, may be included in the estate and divided as part of the divorce settlement.How was the couple’s property divided after the withdrawalThe trial court calculated the couple’s net marital estate at $916,282.81 as of the date Clifford filed for divorce.Its distribution initially showed Clifford receiving $256,488.89 and Valerie receiving $659,793.92. However, those figures did not mean Valerie would permanently retain a substantially larger share of the marital wealth.The court had already accounted for the retirement money Clifford withdrew by treating it as an asset he had received. It then ordered Valerie to make an equalisation payment to him.Under the calculation, Valerie was initially required to pay Clifford $90,960.87 to balance the division. The written order contained a slightly different figure of $90,960.83, a four-cent discrepancy that was not challenged in the appeal.The trial court also found that Clifford owed $9,490 in unpaid child support. That amount was deducted from the equalisation payment, reducing the sum Valerie was required to transfer to $81,470.83.The court concluded that, once the withdrawn retirement funds were taken into account, the division resulted in each spouse receiving half of the marital estate.Valerie nevertheless appealed, arguing that Clifford had not faced an adequate consequence for removing the money and challenging the calculation of his child-support arrears.Why did the appeals court uphold the child-support calculationThe dispute also concerned Clifford’s financial responsibility for the couple’s children during the divorce proceedings.In August 2024, the trial court issued a provisional order giving Valerie primary physical custody, while Clifford received parenting time under Indiana’s guidelines. The court postponed the final decision on child support until the divorce hearing.At the final hearing in May 2025, Clifford was ordered to pay $100 a week in child support and was awarded $100,000 a year. It is based on an arrangement for 116 overnight stays with the children each year.The court calculated support at $9,700 for 97 weeks. After subtracting the $210 Clifford had paid during the proceedings, it decided that he owed $9,490 as of 29 August 2025.But the appellate court found that she had not submitted any evidence about the relevant period at the final hearing. The outcome left the original financial arrangements in place.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Complete and total loser': Trump attacks Bill Maher in 1,300-word Truth Social post after White House dinner
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has launched a fresh attack on comedian Bill Maher, calling him a “complete and total loser” in a lengthy Truth Social post days
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has launched a fresh attack on comedian Bill Maher, calling him a “complete and total loser” in a lengthy Truth Social post days after the two had dinner at the White House, an event Trump had initially described as “great”.The 1,323-word post, which CNN described as Trump's longest-ever social media post based on an analysis, came after Maher mocked the president's approval ratings and made jokes about him during Friday's episode of HBO's Real Time with Bill Maher.Trump began his Sunday post by attacking Maher and the comedian's show, accusing him of dishonesty and questioning the quality of his programme. He also targeted Chuck LaBella, a longtime business partner of Maher, who previously worked on Trump's reality television show The Apprentice.“Let's talk about this COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER, Bill Maher,” Trump wrote, criticising the comedian's ratings and claiming that HBO had lost the quality and popularity it once enjoyed.The president later accused Maher of using a “Laughter Machine” to generate audience reactions, arguing that viewers laughed even when the comedian's remarks were not funny.“Bill Maher lied, but he lies about everything,” Trump wrote, before saying he would no longer watch the programme.Trump disputes Maher's account of White House dinnerThe outburst marked a sharp shift from Trump's public comments following his October 15 dinner with Maher, ESPN host Stephen A. Smith and musician Kid Rock at the White House.The day after the meeting, Trump had described it as a “great dinner” and said he liked Maher, adding that the comedian liked him more than people realised.However, the president's tone changed after Maher discussed the meeting on his HBO show. The comedian joked about Trump's approval ratings and said he had spent four hours at the White House without receiving any compliments from the president about his appearance.Trump disputed the duration of the meeting in his Truth Social post, saying it lasted around two hours or possibly less.“Overall, I thought it was a good meeting,” Trump wrote, adding that he had learned nothing from the conversation and felt it had been a waste of time.Trump also claimed that LaBella had repeatedly contacted him to arrange meetings with Maher and had told him that the comedian respected him.The president recalled their first dinner in March 2025, alleging that Maher had been nervous during the meeting and had appeared with bruising around his eye and nose. Trump also accused the comedian of being dishonest about his views.Maher, meanwhile, had used Friday's programme to make jokes about Trump's political standing and his comments about men's physiques.Trump claims record Republican supportTrump also rejected Maher's remarks about his declining approval ratings, claiming 98% to 99% support among Republicans. However, CNN's October 21 poll put his approval rating among Republicans at 74%, a new low in the network's polling. Trump's figures appeared to refer to a separate poll of self-identified MAGA Republicans.Trump also threatened to have Republicans stop covering Maher, though it was unclear whether he meant Republican guests on the comedian's show or conservative media outlets.Trump considers moving White House reportersTrump also confirmed he was considering relocating White House reporters from their longtime workspace to free up space for other uses.The 1,323-word post surpassed his previous record, a 723-word rant published in May. Factbase, which tracks Trump's social media activity, said it was his longest-ever post across 97,455 posts dating back to 2011.Trump ended with his familiar sign-off: “Thank you for your attention to this matter.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola and her family were hurt in a weekend car crash; an eight-stop Senate campaign tour is delayed days before the November 3 election
articles.summary: Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate challenging Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, and her family suffered minor injuries in a car crash on
articles.body: Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate challenging Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, and her family suffered minor injuries in a car crash on Saturday, forcing her campaign to reschedule events during the final week before the November 3 election.Peltola and her family were travelling to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet when another vehicle struck the car transporting them, her campaign said in a statement on Sunday. Peltola required medical attention following the collision.“Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits,” Cheryl Bruce, Peltola’s campaign manager, said in a statement.“Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover,” Bruce said.Alaska Always Tour: An 8-stop campaign delayedThe crash delayed the start of Peltola’s “Alaska Always Tour”, an eight-stop campaign push planned for the final week before Election Day.Bruce said: “Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families.”According to the Anchorage Police Department, officers responded to a “multi-vehicle collision” at about 6.55pm on Saturday. Peltola’s family and an occupant of a second vehicle were taken to a local hospital with “non-life-threatening injuries”, authorities said. An occupant of a third vehicle refused medical transport.“The circumstances of the collision are under investigation,” the police department said in a statement.Peltola’s campaign said she would resume events on Tuesday, with a stop in Homer, Alaska.Peltola, an Alaska Native and former congresswoman, is challenging incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan for Alaska’s only US Senate seat. She hopes to become the first Democrat in nearly two decades to represent the state in the Senate.What is the row over the Alaska election?The row over Alaska’s November 3 Senate election is about Donald Trump’s administration suing to block certification of the result if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola. The dispute centres on a second candidate with almost the same name as the incumbent. Trump has said he personally ordered the lawsuit.Incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan is running against Democrat Mary Peltola. A second candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg, Alaska, is also running. He has no party affiliation listed on the ballot.Republicans argue that voters intending to support the incumbent could mistakenly vote for the other Sullivan, potentially benefiting Peltola. They have alleged that the second candidate's presence on the ballot is a deliberate attempt to split Republican votes. Daniel J. Sullivan has denied that he is running to confuse voters or coordinating with Democrats.After efforts to remove the second Sullivan from the ballot failed in Alaska's courts, the US Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent the state from certifying the Senate result if the incumbent loses, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion. Trump said he ordered the lawsuit.Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have moved to intervene in the lawsuit and seek its dismissal. Her campaign has called the legal action an attempt to undermine voters' choice.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Andy Burnham leaves door open to referendum on EU free movement
articles.summary: The PM says he wants to start a conversation about potential options for the UK's future relationship with the EU.
articles.body:
The prime minister has left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the European Union.

Asked by broadcasters if he could introduce free movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no", but sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made.

The PM added that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".

Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options, with these expected to be set out around the time of the EU summit next month.

Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.

The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.

The prime minister is thought to be against the idea of leaping quickly to a return to freedom of movement.

Sources indicated no firm decision had been made on whether free movement would need to be rubber-stamped by a referendum.

Burnham is said to believe that a conversation about the UK's future relationship with Brussels needs to happen first.

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement

Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham

Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

The PM has stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

However, he has suggested potential options for the future could range from no changes to the UK-EU relationship, to rejoining the EU customs union, the single market or a new in-out referendum on full EU membership.

In an interview with the Sunday Times , Burnham said he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and the EU.

The PM argued that the type of migration had changed since Brexit, with more foreigners moving permanently.

In contrast, he suggested that when the UK was a member of the EU, migration was "generally younger people", who would spend a few years in the country before returning home.

However, Burnham added: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

The Schengen Agreement, which the UK was not part of when it was in the EU, allows passport-free travel across member countries.

The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.

Burnham has argued that since Brexit, the UK has lost immigration control the country previously had.

"For instance, the small boats crisis has arisen in the last 10 years because we lost that returns agreement when people came here that we could work with other countries to return them," he told broadcasters.

The Conservatives and Reform UK both oppose a return to free movement with the EU.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued most people who voted for Brexit did so because they did not want free movement, while Reform leader Nigel Farage said such a move would be "a total betrayal of Brexit Britain".

However, the Liberal Democrats have argued that allowing freedom of movement would help economic growth.

articles.title: Trump spent about 70 hours on Air Force One in October, with Mike Tyson, Floyd Mayweather and Evander Holyfield among famous guests on separate election trips
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has spent about 70 hours aboard Air Force One so far in October, travelling across the United States to attend rallies and
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has spent about 70 hours aboard Air Force One so far in October, travelling across the United States to attend rallies and campaign for Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.The president’s campaign trips have featured an eclectic mix of passengers, ranging from Cabinet members and senior White House aides to boxing legends and sports personalities.The list of people accompanying Trump offers a glimpse into his inner circle and those who have access to him during the final stretch of the election campaign.According to the Associated Press, political advisers, officials involved in shaping administration policies and communications staff have frequently joined Trump on the trips. Several celebrities have also travelled with the president, making appearances at rallies as the White House seeks to boost Republican candidates.“Who he surrounds himself with are the people he is going to be listening to,” David Cohen, a professor of political science at the University of Akron, said, adding that the people travelling with the president can indicate his priorities.Here is a look at some of the key figures who have travelled with Trump aboard Air Force One this month.Susie Wiles, Stephen Miller among key White House insidersWhite House chief of staff Susie Wiles has been a frequent passenger on Trump’s campaign trips. Wiles, who co-managed Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, recently completed treatment for breast cancer. Trump has described her as the “most powerful woman in the world”.After Trump’s 15th rally in 20 days, Wiles spoke to reporters aboard Air Force One as the plane took off from Greenville, North Carolina, giving the trip a positive assessment.“Great,” she said. “They’ve all been great, honestly.”Other senior administration officials who have travelled with Trump include special envoy Steve Witkoff, deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins.Witkoff has been involved in diplomatic efforts to end the Iran war, which has weighed on Republican prospects ahead of the midterms. Miller, meanwhile, has played a central role in the administration’s immigration crackdown.Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been the most frequent Cabinet member aboard Air Force One during the campaign trips. Lutnick, a billionaire who previously ran financial services firm Cantor Fitzgerald, has known Trump since the 1990s.During rallies, Lutnick has highlighted new factory investments and business projects that the president has cited to argue that the US economy is performing well.Bill Pulte, director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, has joined Trump for at least five legs of the campaign tour. His frequent presence suggests he has considerable access to the president beyond what his formal position might indicate.Pulte, whose family is associated with a homebuilding company, briefly served as acting director of national intelligence and oversaw layoffs in that office. He has also led pressure campaigns against Federal Reserve officials Jerome Powell and Lisa Cook.He previously floated the idea of replacing the traditional 30-year mortgage with a 50-year option, a proposal that has since been abandoned.Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr has also accompanied Trump, including during a lengthy West Coast trip on October 13 and 14. Carr has sought to use the agency’s regulatory authority over broadcast networks to challenge their coverage of the president.Aides, speechwriters and political strategists travel with TrumpTrump’s travelling entourage also includes several aides who help manage his schedule, communications and campaign messaging.Natalie Harp, an executive assistant who accompanies the president on most of his trips, is among the regular passengers. Walt Nauta, director of Oval Office Operations, and his deputy, Chamberlain Harris, have also travelled frequently with Trump.Harris additionally serves on the Commission of Fine Arts, one of the government bodies involved in reviewing Trump’s White House ballroom project and other construction plans.Despite Trump’s preference for improvising during public appearances, speechwriting director Ross Worthington has repeatedly joined him aboard Air Force One this month.Trump’s campaign speeches have included a promise of $5,000 checks if Republicans retain control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate after the November 3 elections. He has also highlighted proposed factory projects and investments in communities he visits.Communications adviser Margo Martin, who regularly posts videos of Trump on social media, has accompanied the president, as has White House communications director Steven Cheung.Katie Zacharia, who served as White House press secretary for five days, spent two days travelling with Trump during a trip that included Alaska, Nevada, Arizona and Montana.The campaign entourage also includes political strategists working on Republican election prospects. Matt Brasseaux, Trump’s political director and a former Republican National Committee staffer, has been part of the travelling group.Johnny DeStefano, a senior aide during Trump’s first term who temporarily returned to the White House this summer to work on midterm strategy, has also been seen aboard Air Force One. Former White House deputy chief of staff James Blair has joined the trips as well.The presence of these officials gives Trump access to advisers and aides during long flights between campaign stops, allowing political planning and discussions to continue while he travels.Mike Tyson, Floyd Mayweather and other celebrities join campaign tripsTrump has also brought several well-known sports personalities aboard Air Force One as he campaigns for Republicans in potentially difficult midterm races.Boxing champions Mike Tyson, Floyd Mayweather Jr and Evander Holyfield have all travelled with the president on separate occasions. Tyson and Holyfield have a notorious history: during their 1997 heavyweight championship bout, Tyson bit off a piece of Holyfield’s right ear.The two former champions did not travel aboard Air Force One at the same time.Martha Kumar, a professor at Towson University who studies presidential communications, said campaign travel can be stressful and that presidents often appreciate having people around who can help them relax.“You want to have people around you that make you feel comfortable,” Kumar said. “When you think about it, it is really stressful. You want some relief.”Rapper Nicki Minaj was also featured in a video posted by Cheung on Sunday, in which the communications director interviewed her aboard Air Force One as Trump travelled to Michigan for a campaign rally. Minaj praised the president.The White House has sought to include celebrities at campaign stops, using their appearances to attract attention and add star power to Trump’s efforts to mobilise Republican voters.Other personalities who have travelled with Trump include retired NASCAR champion Richard Petty, who accompanied him to North Carolina; former NFL coach Jon Gruden, who travelled to Ohio; and retired NFL running back Todd Gurley, who joined a trip to Georgia.Influencer-turned-boxer Jake Paul has also travelled with the president. These celebrities have made appearances at Trump’s rallies during the campaign tour.Republican lawmakers also join Trump aboard Air Force OneBeyond administration officials, political advisers and celebrities, Trump’s aircraft has carried lawmakers as the president seeks to help Republicans retain control of Congress.Jeff Freeland, the White House liaison with the House of Representatives, has travelled with the president alongside several lawmakers.Republican Representative William Timmons of South Carolina has joined the trips, as have Texas Representatives Beth Van Duyne and Brandon Gill. Other House members who have travelled with Trump include Brian Jack of Georgia, Tim Moore of North Carolina and Anna Paulina Luna of Florida.Senator John Barrasso of Wyoming, the second-ranking Republican in the Senate, has flown with Trump multiple times this month.Texas Senator Ted Cruz has also accompanied the president. Cruz, who previously sought the Republican presidential nomination, is among the political figures considering the 2028 presidential race.With the November 3 midterms approaching, Trump’s travel schedule has become a key part of the Republican campaign effort. His rallies are intended to energise voters, promote his administration’s economic agenda and support candidates seeking to preserve the party’s congressional majorities.You use AI every day.
