articles.title: A San Francisco mansion held by one family for more than 40 years was listed for $18.5 million on 2 October; just 20 days later, the Presidio property sold for $28.5 million, a record $10 million over the asking price
articles.summary: Homes selling above their asking prices are not uncommon in San Francisco’s luxury real estate market, but one recent sale has set a city record.
articles.body: Homes selling above their asking prices are not uncommon in San Francisco’s luxury real estate market, but one recent sale has set a city record. An eight-bedroom mansion at 20 Cherry St. on Presidio Wall sold for $28.5 million on Thursday, 22 October, fetching $10 million more than its $18.5 million asking price after just 20 days on the market, according to the San Francisco Business Times. The buyer’s identity has not been disclosed. Nina Hatvany of Compass represented the buyer.A rare sale after four decadesThe house, at the end of a cul-de-sac on the edge of the Presidio, sits on about 0.31 acres, which is a large lot for this part of the city. Built in 1966, this mid-century house was designed by the Whisler-Patri architectural firm. The listing on Redfin describes the house as having an ‘impressively forward-thinking design’ and being a ‘beautiful integration of dramatic spaces seamlessly connecting with the outdoors’.The eight-bedroom, seven-bathroom house comes with seven parking spaces, including a three-car garage. The listing describes it as an ‘extraordinary estate’ and a ‘rare opportunity to find a home with such a massive footprint’.The property remained with one family for more than 40 years, according to the publication. The sellers were the Janice R. Lurie Trust and the Robert A. Lurie Trust. The property came on the market after Janice Rosen Lurie, the long-time resident and former wife of former San Francisco Giants owner Bob Lurie, died in July aged 96. Her family’s decision to sell came after decades of ownership, and the sale now marks the end of a long chapter for the house.‘Everything is clearly in the right place! Fantastic opportunity for a new owner to create their legacy,’ the listing says.The home went on the market on 2 October at $18.5 million. The sale closed on 22 October, according to the listing. Nina Hatvany of Compass represented the buyer, who has not been publicly identified. The final price was $28.5 million, which was $10 million above the asking price, or about 54% more. Hatvany told the publication that the large lot, private garden and views towards the Presidio make the property particularly rare. Those features, more than the house itself, seem to have driven the bidding.The $10 million gap is the largest dollar overbid the city has recorded. In May, a Cow Hollow home at 2512 Union St. sold for $15 million after being listed for $7.95 million, a premium of roughly 88.7%. The gap was smaller in dollar terms but far larger as a share of the asking price.Earlier this month, a house at 2 Sixth Ave., near the Presidio, sold for $15 million after being listed for $8 million. That $7 million premium falls between the two extremes. Taken together, the three sales show how sellers in the top tier of the market have been able to push prices well beyond their initial asking prices.The average 30-year mortgage rate rose above 7% earlier this month. For many buyers who need a loan, that is a serious obstacle. The most expensive homes, however, have felt far less of that pressure. About 79% of San Francisco homes selling for more than $7 million had no mortgage at closing as of 1 September.The luxury market has been particularly strong as wealth from the artificial intelligence industry flows into the city.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Fans of the book series A Court of Thorns and Roses are planning parties and taking days off work, ahead of a new edition being released at 00:01 GMT on Tuesday.

Dozens will be gathering at Wolverhampton Arts Centre on Monday night, to celebrate the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony.

"It's the escapism, it's a way for people to escape from every day life. So many people, especially young women, see themselves in these characters and there are so many really strong messages about empowerment and finding strength," party organiser Holly Fellows, from Redditch, said.

The fantasy series, written by American author, Sarah J. Maas, is popular with readers across the world.

To pass the time until the book goes on sale fans will take part in arts and crafts projects.

"Waterstones Wolverhampton will be bringing the books, and bang on midnight everyone will receive their book and we will spend some quiet time reading," Fellows said.

"I've booked the day off work [tomorrow]. I'll be undisturbed for the whole day, and I reckon I'll get through it by the evening."

ACOTAR is a fantasy romance series, set in the fictional world of Prythian.

There have been five books in the series so far, A Court of Thorns and Roses (2015), A Court of Mist and Fury (2016), A Court of Wings and Ruin (2017), A Court of Frost and Starlight (2018), and A Court of Silver Flames (2021).

In 2015, ACOTAR was ranked a 'Most Read Book of the Year' on book recommendation site, Goodreads.

The books have millions of fans, with the hashtag ACOTAR being used 2.1 million times on the social media app TikTok, and 1.8 million times on Instagram.

Millions of fans have been posting on social media sharing their excitement ahead of the release - with some getting their hands on the book early.

One posted on TikTok saying: "Why did I waste my annual leave on important life events, when there's a new acotar coming out".

Another said: "I simply don't know if I'm ready for this".

It has been five years since the last edition was released, something Fellows said has left fans "going crazy".

"It's created this sense of community that - just from a book - is this massive magical world.

"Where I work, there are women who are my age reading them, there's also women in their 40s, 50s that are picking them up. Online I'm seeing loads of men reading them. It's a universal craze to be honest."

The author confirmed on her website that after the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony on 27 October, the seventh book in the series, A Court of Forgotten Melody, will be released on 12 January 2027.

articles.title: Chris Brown: US singer given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack
articles.summary: The R&B star previously pleaded guilty to affray, after attacking a music producer with a glass bottle.
articles.body:
The R&B star was given an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, over the attack at private members' club Tape in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023.

Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Both men, who had pleaded guilty to affray, were also ordered to pay £1,500 costs.

Judge Tony Baumgartner said Brown's use of the glass bottle to hit the victim twice over the head "was plainly dangerous", adding that the violence of the attack was "intense".

The sentence means Brown will not be imprisoned unless he commits another offence during the 12-month period of suspension.

The court heard Brown's attack on music producer Abraham 'Abe' Diaw left the victim in need of hospital treatment for his injuries.

In sentencing, Judge Baumgartner said: "The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained."

CCTV footage was shown where Brown struck Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head, and then hitting his shoulder.

Sentencing Brown, Judge Baumgartner said: "This was not planned violence. It was nevertheless serious violence by two people in a crowded nightclub."

The judge told Brown: "Violence of this kind in a crowded nightclub is serious, it creates an obvious risk, not only to the person against whom it is directed, but also to others nearby."

He added that Brown's conduct was "particularly dangerous" and that he had to be "physically pulled away" from the attack.

The judge said Brown's fame, commercial success and professional standing "do not entitle you to special treatment - the law applies equally to everyone".

But judge Baumgartner also said he had noted Brown's guilty plea, compliance with bail conditions, and the impact a custodial sentence would have on Brown's children, and said the singer's "risk of further offending is low".

Brown and Akinlolu pleaded guilty to a charge of affray at Southwark Crown Court in July.

The singer had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied, and which were subsequently dropped.

These were assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon.

Following Brown and Akinlolu's guilty pleas, the CPS released a statement outlining that Brown had approached Diaw on the dance floor, hitting him over the head with a glass bottle twice, before Akinlolu then punched Diaw in the head.

"They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club," the CPS said. "The victim was kicked while he was seated defenceless on the floor."

On Monday, the court was shown three pieces of CCTV footage from inside Tape nightclub on the night of the attack.

The attack lasted no more than 20 seconds, but Brown could be seen hitting the victim four times with a tequila bottle, twice to the head.

Prosecutor, Heidi Stonecliffe KC, described the weapon as a "heavy square-shaped tequila bottle" and said Diaw was approached by Brown at around 03:00.

The footage showed that the nightclub was very small and packed at the time.

The defence described Chris Brown as a "dedicated and a loving father of four children," someone who is "positive and present".

The singer is described as having lived "a good and law-abiding life" since his last conviction in 2013.

The events in Tape nightclub were described by the defence as a "short and deeply regretted incident".

Brown's defence lawyer told the court that he apologises to all those present at the club at the time of the attack.

"This is an ugly and unattractive incident," Sallie Bennett-Jenkins KC said.

"It is, however, an incident which was very short-lived, lasting something more than 17 seconds but no more than 20.

"It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr Brown... offers a profound apology to all those present."

The court heard Akinlolu "genuinely believed" that Brown was "under attack" when he joined the attack, punching Diaw.

Brown was described as being like a "brother" to Akinlolu, his lawyer Laurie-Anne Power KC told the court.

She added: "He genuinely believed him to be under attack and became involved, and thereafter accepts his initial involvement very quickly evolved into the events he has pleaded guilty to."

Diaw was taken to St Mary's Hospital in London after the attack. Ms Stonecliffe KC said he was discharged with "pain relief and a diagnosis of head injury and superficial injury of the knee".

An MRI scan taken in early March showed a "high grade injury to a ligament on the inner side of the left knee", the court heard.

Defending Brown, Ms Bennett-Jenkins KC said there was a "relatively low level of force" and disputed how significant the injuries were.

The defence argued that the attack left no fractures or broken skin and there was an absence of serious injuries.

Diaw, the victim, was "not supportive of the prosecution" and "withdrew" his support some time after the incident, the court heard.

Brown and Akinlolu stood up and faced one another and clasped hands after the judge concluded his sentencing remarks before walking out of the glass dock.

There were loud cheers outside the court as Chris Brown left the building as he appeared to stop to sign an autograph.

After the sentencing, Brown shared a video from inside his car on his Instagram story, showing him looking out the window before turning to the camera and giving a thumbs-up.

Affray is an offence under the Public Order Act and a person is deemed guilty in law if they use or threaten "unlawful violence towards another" with their behaviour, leading someone to fear for their personal safety.

Brown, 37, is considered one of the biggest stars in R&B, with a string of hit songs including Turn Up The Music, Ayo, Freaky Friday, Run It, Forever, Yeah 3x and Don't Wake Me Up.

articles.title: Alaska’s Koyukuk gold rush drew about 70 steamers upriver in 1898 and produced over $4 million by 1918, yet most boomtowns vanished as the region’s population fell by 1921
articles.summary: Alaska Koyukuk gold rush history begins in 1898, when about seventy small steamers carried prospectors up the Koyukuk River through practically unknown
articles.body: Alaska Koyukuk gold rush history begins in 1898, when about seventy small steamers carried prospectors up the Koyukuk River through practically unknown country. Most of the boomtowns that sprang up in 1898 and 1899 have since disappeared, leaving Wiseman, Coldfoot and the ghost town of Old Bettles as the survivors. The gold itself was real, placer mining, which recovers gold from loose gravel, produced more than $4 million by 1918. Few individual miners cleared more than $50,000, yet a larger share of them made between $5,000 and $50,000 than in any other Alaskan district. Most streams there yielded coarse gold.How a fleet of about seventy small steamers pushed 600 miles up the Koyukuk River in 1898A 1921 article in The Pathfinder magazine, republished by the National Park Service, describes the fleet as loaded with prospectors, most of whom owned their boats. The majority came from the eastern United States, with a scattering of experienced old-timers among them. The account credits those old-timers with getting the fleet 600 miles or more up the river, as far as the sites of today’s towns of Bergman and Bettles.Many of the easterners were unused to the hardships of such a journey and discouraged by the desolate look of the country. They gave up almost at once and headed home before winter arrived. Some abandoned their boats and took passage downstream with others, while some left theirs in the care of braver friends who stayed to try their luck. As a result, the bleached remains of little steamers could still be seen here and there along the riverbanks.Streams named for loved ones back home, and the first creeks that proved the gravel held goldEnough men stayed to show that the gravels of the Koyukuk and its tributaries were not barren. Far from home, the prospectors named streams after mothers, sisters and sweethearts, which is how Myrtle Creek, Clara Creek and Rosie Creek got their names.Myrtle Creek and Emma Creek were among the first to be prospected, and together they are said to have produced more than $100,000 in their first few years, with some gold coming out ever since. Myrtle Creek feeds Slate Creek, the stream on which the town of Coldfoot now stands. Gold Creek and Gold Bench, both feeding the South Fork of the Koyukuk, gave up more than a quarter of a million dollars in their first four years but have been light producers since.Nolan Creek and the Hammond River, the richest ground, the biggest nuggets and a $400,000 stretchNolan Creek and its tributaries are described as probably the richest and most consistent producers in the whole region. Gold was first found there in the autumn of 1903, and about $25,000 was taken out that winter. Another $140,000 followed in the winter of 1904 to 1905, and the creek, its tributaries and its benches (raised gravel terraces beside the stream) have produced steadily since. One stretch of ground only about 400 feet long, between claims three and four below Discovery claim, yielded around $400,000. The largest nugget found in the valley was worth $865, and a $714 nugget turned up on a bench the summer before the article was written.The Hammond River, a tributary of the Middle Fork, followed a slower path. Gold was found there in the autumn of 1901, but the rich pay in deep ground was not struck until 1912. About $1 million then came out of the valley over four years. The largest nugget from the main river weighed about 150 ounces and sold for $2,700.Why the fortune faded: Scattered gold, soaring supply costs and a shrinking population by 1921Gold on the Koyukuk never came in one dependable ribbon. The 1921 article says no continuous paystreak, meaning the richest band of gold-bearing gravel, was found anywhere in the district. It could be picked up in one place on a claim and followed for a while before disappearing, then turn up again in another direction after systematic prospecting.Mascot Creek shows the pattern. Pay was struck there in the autumn of 1902, and over $100,000 was taken from the creek bed by open-cutting the following summer. Output later fell so far that the men still working it made little more than a living. Porcupine Creek went the other way: considerable work in 1901 found no decided paystreak, yet in the four years before 1921 it became a good producer.Costs did the rest. By 1921 the Koyukuk’s population was smaller than at any time since 1902, which the account blames on the high price of supplies and transport. Many old-timers had left to help build the government railroad, and the hope was that cheaper freight once it was finished would draw them back, along with newcomers, to mine on a larger scale than ever before.You use AI every day. articles.title: Liam Payne donated nearly £10,000 to children’s fundraisers during one video call; his cousin is now continuing that spirit through a tribute song
articles.summary: A song written in memory of Liam Payne is being used to continue the former One Direction singer’s charitable giving.
articles.body: A song written in memory of Liam Payne is being used to continue the former One Direction singer’s charitable giving. His cousin, Ross Harris, wrote Bones after Payne died aged 31 on 16 October 2024 and later built The Bones Fund around the song’s master royalties. The initiative combines those royalties with direct donations and merchandise profits, with the money intended for causes Payne supported during his life. Its inspiration came from a late-night video call in summer 2024, when the cousins browsed online fundraising pages and found children whose fundraising pots needed completing. According to the fund’s website, Payne donated nearly £10,000 to young people that night before his bank began blocking further payments. Harris has since sought to carry that spirit of giving forward through the song and the fund.How Ross Harris turned Bones into The Bones FundHarris wrote Bones with Jordan Round as an outlet for his grief after Payne’s death. The song came out at the end of August 2025, shortly after what would have been Payne’s 32nd birthday. In an Instagram post reported by Rolling Stone on 1 September 2025, Harris described the track as the most personal song he had written and explained that creating it had helped him process his loss. Rolling Stone and the fund’s website say the song’s artwork features a rose drawn by Payne himself. The idea behind the fund drew on the cousins’ earlier FaceTime call. During the conversation, they browsed JustGiving and GoFundMe pages, looking for children whose fundraising pots needed completing. The fund’s website says Payne made donations totalling nearly £10,000 that night. Harris later decided to use the song’s earnings to continue the kind of giving they had done on that call.In late August 2026, a year after the original release, Harris released an acoustic version to formally launch the fund. The fund’s website says royalties from both versions contribute to its pool of money, alongside donations and merchandise proceeds. The website explains that The Bones Project Ltd owns the master rights to Bones, which Harris gifted to the company. Master royalties collected through its distributor, DistroKid, go into the fund.How streaming, donations and merchandise support the fundThe Bones Fund’s website displays a running counter for streams and estimated royalties. The figures are estimates, with the site explaining that totals are updated as documented streaming figures and royalty payments come in. The website says master royalties from the song are directed to the fund, alongside direct donations and merchandise profits. Supporters can contribute directly through the fund’s website, with payments processed by Stripe. Merchandise offers another source of income, with products including tote bags, mugs, magnets and stickers printed to order. The website gives two descriptions of how merchandise profits are used. One says around 60% to 70% of the profit on each item is donated, while another says every penny of profit goes to charity. These statements differ, and the site does not explain the discrepancy.Is The Bones Fund a registered charity, and which causes does it support?The Bones Fund is not currently a registered charity. Its website identifies it as the trading name of The Bones Project Ltd, a company limited by guarantee registered in England and Wales. The organisation says it intends to apply to the Charity Commission for charitable status when it is able to do so. A company limited by guarantee has no shareholders and does not pay dividends. The fund says it operates on a non-profit basis, with money intended for the causes it supports. It also says some funds may be used for necessary running costs, including website hosting, marketing and legal expenses.Until it obtains registered charitable status, the company says it cannot offer Gift Aid on donations. Payments processed through Stripe are also subject to processing fees. The fund’s website names UNICEF, Soccer Aid and the Trussell Trust among the organisations connected to Payne’s charitable work. It presents the project as a way to continue supporting causes he worked with, raised money for or donated to during his life and career. The money raised is intended to be distributed to the different causes Payne supported.The website says the fund will report back with as much information as possible about the money raised and where it goes. Payne’s family also asked for donations to Great Ormond Street Hospital Charity instead of funeral flowers. In October 2025, the Express & Star reported that almost £250,000 had been raised in his memory, citing a source who said most contributions had been made privately. For Harris, the project links a personal tribute to a practical way of helping others. The song began as an outlet for grief, while the fund draws on a memory of Payne giving money to children whose fundraising campaigns needed support. Through the song, its acoustic version, donations and merchandise, Harris hopes to keep his cousin’s generosity alive.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Storm Boelo made our Blackpool wedding day special, couple say
articles.summary: Leigh and Paul Hutchinson unexpectedly had their first dance in the iconic Blackpool Tower ballroom.
articles.body:
A couple whose wedding day coincided with Storm Boelo said last-minute changes caused by the weather did not ruin their day, "it made it".

Leigh and Paul Hutchinson had planned to surprise their wedding guests with a glass of fizz at the top of Blackpool Tower, but high winds forced the venue to close the area.

Instead, staff arranged a private bar on the upper balcony of the Tower Ballroom and later cleared the dance floor so the newlyweds could share their first dance there.

"They did something really special for us," Leigh said. "It made the day so much more than we could have ever imagined."

The couple met 10 years ago and decided they wanted a low-key wedding at the chapel next door to The Beach House where they met.

Leigh said: "It was just going to be us. A quick wedding and a meal with family afterwards. So it spiralled to say the least."

After the ceremony, the bride, groom and wedding guests walked down the Prom in the storm.

Leigh said: "I don't know how we made it! We caused quite a stir. I think there's still a few brollies missing."

Later, when one of the guests suggested it would be nice to dance in the Tower Ballroom, staff cleared the dance floor to let them.

"They played the organ and we had the most magical first dance," Leigh said.

"We were really overwhelmed with everyone's comments and cheers. It was incredible."

Groom Paul joked that if he had known his first dance would take place on one of the most iconic dance floors in the world, "he wouldn't have turned up".

"I was nervous dancing in front of 40 people, never mind hundreds I didn't know, but it made the day," he said.

"It was full and there were a lot of good dancers in there too."

Rob Smith, general manager of Blackpool Tower, said: "It was a special moment and one our team will never forget.

"The Tower Ballroom is one of the most famous venues in the world and Leigh and Paul are now part of its history.

"We wish them both all the very best for the future."

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) on Monday labelled the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) an “evil force” following the arrest of DMK leader and former Tamil Nadu school education minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi in connection with an alleged Rs 100-crore scam.The Chennai Police’s Central Crime Branch (CCB) arrested Poyyamozhi over alleged irregularities in granting recognition and other statutory clearances to private schools during his tenure as school education minister.“Is the mask of the DMK—which once arrogantly boasted, ‘We are the banyan tree; no matter who governs, we are the ruling party’—finally being torn off today? The history of this ‘landlord-style’ party is one of proclaiming ‘principles are our lifeblood’ from public platforms while simultaneously using its power to plunder the people’s tax money!” the TVK’s IT wing wrote in Tamil in a post on X.“In the days to come, people will speak of the DMK not just as an ‘evil force,’ but as the very fountainhead of corruption! articles.title: Why do people overpay for used cars with mileage just below round numbers? Researchers examining Texas car transactions found that dealers earned $46 to $168 extra at certain mileage thresholds.
articles.summary: Research reveals that used car dealers earn up to $168 more for vehicles with mileage just below round numbers, exploiting buyer psychology while consumers remain unaware.
articles.body: A used car that has travelled 49,900 miles may seem like a better deal than one showing 50,000 miles on its odometer. Although the difference is only a hundred miles, that small change in the numbers can make the vehicle appear significantly more attractive to buyers. And used-car dealers may be benefiting from this buyer perception.According to a new study conducted by Andreas Kraft of the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and Raghunath Singh Rao of the University of Texas at Austin, dealerships earned significantly higher profits on cars whose odometer readings fell just below round-number mileage thresholds. The findings highlight how a psychological tendency to focus on the first digit of a number can influence purchasing decisions, sometimes at a cost to customers.The study was published in the Journal of Marketing Research in February 2026 and examined how consumers’ attention to numbers can shape prices, sales and the way businesses operate. The cars with mileage readings below the thresholds were sold at considerably higher prices, so the question arises: Are the cars being sold on the basis of quality or dealers’ business acumen?What is the left-digit effect?The phenomenon at the centre of the research is known as left-digit bias, which describes the tendency to pay disproportionate attention to the leftmost digit of a number while giving less consideration to the digits that follow.This is something that consumers encounter on a regular basis. For example, a product priced at $1.99 can appear cheaper than a product listed at $2, even though the difference is really insignificant. But that is where human psychology comes into play. Although the difference is just one cent, the change in the first digit can make us feel as though we have crossed a forbidden boundary.The same pattern works here. A vehicle showing 49,900 miles looks as if it has been used less than a vehicle with 50,000 miles, although the difference is just 100 miles. The former is often perceived, and presented to customers, as a car with lower mileage, despite the relatively small difference in the readings.Because mileage is such an important consideration when buying a car, the study suggests that buyers may sometimes attach disproportionate importance to round-number thresholds rather than considering the complete odometer reading.What did the researchers discover?To investigate this behaviour, Kraft and Rao analysed 4.8 million used-car transactions recorded by the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles between 2014 and 2021. The dataset represented approximately 10% of used-car sales across the United States during the period.The researchers compared cars with mileage readings just below and just above the thresholds to examine their prices. They found that dealers earned an estimated $46 to $168 more on vehicles just below certain mileage thresholds.These findings suggest that the difference is not merely about how consumers perceive mileage. It can influence the prices dealers charge, the vehicles they choose to stock and how quickly those vehicles sell.How dealers benefit from the biasThe researchers describe this process as behavioural skimming, in which businesses benefit from consumers who are less attentive to certain details.Although dealers’ charges also depend on the services and convenience they offer, the left-digit effect creates an additional advantage for vehicles with mileage readings just below round numbers. Buyers who focus heavily on the first digit may perceive these vehicles as better value and be willing to pay more for them.This actually creates a very interesting market dynamic. Rather than competition between dealerships automatically eliminating the pricing advantage, the researchers found that consumer inattention could sustain it. It makes consumers think they are guiding prices, but it is the dealers who benefit by giving them a sense of choice between prices.What used-car buyers should keep in mindThe findings do not mean that mileage is irrelevant when purchasing a used vehicle. Higher mileage can indicate greater wear, although a car’s maintenance record, age, driving conditions and mechanical condition must also be considered when making a purchase.Consumers must pay attention to the complete number rather than allowing the leftmost digit to determine whether a car is worth buying. Comparing similar vehicles across dealerships and private listings can help you find your dream vehicle at a more reasonable price.The broader lesson extends beyond cars. From supermarket discounts to product pricing and electric-vehicle range figures, numbers can influence purchasing decisions in ways consumers may not always recognise.Sometimes, the difference between a good deal and an expensive mistake is not the number itself, but how we read it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Vijay Deverakonda, Rashmika Mandanna file cybercrime complaint in Hyderabad over online trolling after Koffee With Karan
articles.summary: HYDERABAD: Days after their Koffee With Karan appearance sparked a wave of online criticism over their relationship, actors Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika
articles.body: HYDERABAD: Days after their Koffee With Karan appearance sparked a wave of online criticism over their relationship, actors Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna have approached Hyderabad Cyber Crime authorities with a formal complaint against allegedly fabricated online claims, manipulated screenshots and targeted harassment.The move comes amid a public response from both actors, who took to Instagram on Monday to defend their relationship and hit back at trolls, with Rashmika calling out what she described as misleading narratives and Vijay declaring that the couple was “gloriously happy”.The couple's team has sought an impartial probe into specific online publications and digital material circulating across social media platforms.The complaint reportedly identifies alleged false narratives, fabricated content, manipulated screenshots, impersonation and targeted online harassment. Relevant links and supporting evidence have been submitted to the authorities for examination.The team said it hoped “the matter will be investigated in accordance with the law and that the deliberate creation and circulation of misleading narratives, including any coordinated or paid campaigns established through evidence, will be addressed appropriately.”“Every identified instance of publishing, reposting or amplifying potentially unlawful content may be examined on its own merits. Appropriate legal remedies will be pursued wherever warranted, in accordance with due process,” a statement by Vijay's team read.However, an official confirmation from the police regarding the complaint is still awaited.Earlier on Monday afternoon, Vijay and Rashmika addressed the ongoing controversy through separate Instagram posts.Vijay described Rashmika as his best friend and wife, expressing happiness over their relationship and dismissing the criticism directed at them."My best friend, my wife, my woman. One of the most beautiful parts of my life that I got absolutely right. For all those concerned, We are both gloriously happy. I am blessed. If its me and her against the world - so be it. Big love to all those who celebrate love and the simplicity of living happily. Now, with absolutely no intended kindness or respect, everyone else can go fuck themselves," Vijay's post read.Rashmika Mandanna says online backlash feels like an ‘angry mob’Before Vijay's post, Rashmika had addressed the controversy in an Instagram note, saying the reaction to their interview had gone beyond people expressing differing opinions."My lil' 2 cents on this whole issue concerning me and Vijju. I generally don't address these things because everyone has a right to their opinions. Sometimes, I even enjoy reading them and gaining a different perspective. But the current frenzy over our interview feels less like people having opinions and more like an angry mob looking for someone to vent at. Somewhere along the way, the whole point got lost. Maybe it didn't fit your lens. Maybe some of you simply don't want to see it. I'm writing this because I want to protect the people who believe in love, and I hope everyone gets to find their own version of it," she posted.Since the episode aired last week, the couple has faced online trolling over several revelations about their relationship. Clips from the episode circulated on social media, drawing mixed reactions from users.One moment that attracted particular attention was Vijay's revelation that Rashmika had to propose to him nearly 100 times before he agreed to marry her. Several social media users reacted by labelling Vijay a “red flag”.Addressing the discussion, Rashmika said the conversation was not about the number of proposals or how long it took for them to decide to get married. She explained that Vijay wanted time to think through the practical aspects of their future before making the decision."We've been bombarded with opinions, comments and unsolicited advice on all our profiles, mine and yours, unnecessarily. The conviction with which people came at us genuinely shook me a little. I was like, WHAT THE FK IS GOING ON? So I took a step back, thought about it, and here's my lil' take on my own life. First, it was never about the number of times or an entire year. That's where some of you got stuck. ""Yes, that conversation happened. But neither of us was looking for a grand proposal. The conversation was about him wanting both of us to take the time and space to understand each other, to be sure that despite all the highs and lows, the joys and stresses of life, this was what we wanted and the right time for it.And we did. We chose each other.It's okay that I knew exactly what I wanted. And it was equally okay that he wanted time to think all the practical things of life through and be sure. That didn't change our love in any way.""I am all heart and he is the thinker- and we need that in each other's lives. For us, marriage was never about a proposal, getting down on one knee or putting a ring on a finger. That's the decorative part. For us, it was about building a life and a future together.And I think we did that beautifully so far," she added.Rashmika also defended her expression of affection for Vijay, questioning why being deeply attached to one's partner should be viewed negatively."Find someone you would go to any lengths for, someone who would do the same for you. And yes, I am OBSESSED with my man. When did that become a bad thing? If I'm not IN LOVE with the man I'm marrying, then why in the world would I marry him? He's going to be my companion for life.""My friend through the ordinary days and the extraordinary ones. The father of my children. The man I grow old with. Find a man who loves you so beautifully that even after you're married, you'd still want to tell him, 'Let's get married.' I would do it a thousand times - 100 is nothing. It's really that simple," she wrote.Rashmika also urged social media users to refrain from speaking ill of her family, arguing that personal choices should not become a reason for online attacks."Bitch about me all you want. I can take it. But talking about my family without knowing them? That's not feminism. That's bullying dressed up as feminism. Feminism was never about putting someone else down or establishing superiority, whether you're a man or a woman. It was always about having the freedom to choose your own life and taking charge of it. I took charge of mine," she expressed.In the latter part of her note, Rashmika spoke about Vijay's support through difficult moments in her life and said she was happy with her marriage. She also criticised the circulation of what she described as misleading edits and false online narratives about their relationship."Right now, I am the happiest I have ever been. And I hope you can see that in my face, in the joy I've felt since getting married, in my performances, in my films, and simply in the way I live my life.I am happy. I am content. I am blessed. And the fact that some people would rather believe random narratives, misleading edits and absolute lies created on the internet that believe what I say about my own life is honestly a little creepy.""When I snap a bone, you aren't there. He is. When my stomach hurts every month, you aren't there. He is. When I need to go to the hospital, you aren't there. He is. When I wake up in the middle of the night with anxiety, you aren't there. He is. And when I break down, I don't have your shoulder to cry on. I have his. So please, don't worry about me or him. I genuinely wish and pray that you find someone you love who loves you just as deeply. And if that isn't what you want for yourself, that's completely fine too. Live the life that makes you happy," she said.Rashmika concluded her note by thanking fans who have continued to support her over the years, including her Kannadiga fans."And it rewarded me with immense love ....And to some of my Kannadiga friends... Ahhh, how lovely it is to know that I'm still so deeply etched in your hearts even after 10 years. For you to still be celebrating me after all this time... truly, I'm blessed! Love to all those who celebrate love and joy. And to everyone else... please find something that makes you happy, too," she signed off.Rashmika Mandanna and Vijay Deverakonda tied the knot in Udaipur on February 26, 2026.(With ANI inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Hyderabad | Silver Rate in Hyderabad | Bank Holidays in Hyderabad | Public Holidays in Hyderabad | Hyderabad AQI | Weather in Hyderabad | Petrol Price in Hyderabad | Diesel Price in Hyderabad | CNG Price in Hyderabad | LPG Price in HyderabadStay updated with the latest Hyderabad news. articles.title: ECI orders suspension of 6 officers, action against 21 others over Agra MLC poll lapses
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Monday ordered the immediate suspension of six officers, including two sector magistrates and four
articles.body: LUCKNOW: The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Monday ordered the immediate suspension of six officers, including two sector magistrates and four police personnel, for supervisory lapses during polling in the Agra Division Teachers’ constituency of the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council.The commission also directed disciplinary proceedings against other polling personnel deployed at polling stations 21 and 26, where repolling was held on Monday.In a letter dated October 26 to UP chief electoral officer Navdeep Rinwa, ECI secretary Suman Kumar Das said officers entrusted with supervisory responsibilities had failed to ensure effective supervision and maintain proper control within and around the polling stations.The commission observed that such dereliction of duty by supervisory officers was serious and could not be condoned.At polling station 21 in Saiyan, the commission ordered the suspension of sector magistrate OP Chak, sector police officer Inspector Hariharan Singh and sub-inspector Sandeep Kumar.At polling station 26 in Fatehabad, sector magistrate Vishal Rathore, Inspector Purushottam Pal and sub-inspector Sumit Tyagi also face suspension.The commission directed the authorities to issue chargesheets against the six officers and forward draft chargesheets to the ECI for vetting within 10 days.Disciplinary proceedings were also ordered against five presiding officers, three polling officers, five head constables and 11 constables deployed at the two polling stations, in accordance with the divisional commissioner’s inquiry findings.An immediate compliance report has been sought.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: Part of Antarctica named after former BBC reporter Jonathan Amos
articles.summary: A stretch of water in the west of the continent is now called the Amos Channel after the ex-BBC journalist.
articles.body:
Part of Antarctica has been named after former BBC science correspondent Jonathan Amos.

A stretch of water between Rothschild Island and Alexander Island in the west of the White Continent is now called the Amos Channel.

Amos was given the honour for his "exceptional and influential role in bringing Antarctic research to the forefront of public understanding" during his 38-year career at BBC News, the naming committee said.

The channel is a new feature in Antarctica that appeared when a chunk of ice that connected Rothschild and Alexander Islands disintegrated.

The melting ice sheets of this remote continent are just one of many aspects of polar science that Amos reported on while at the BBC. He also covered colossal icebergs , the fate of penguin colonies and a BBC exclusive about the discovery of Ernest Shackleton's lost ship , the Endurance.

"It's absolutely incredible - what an extraordinary accolade. I'm so touched that there's a little bit of Antarctica named after me," Amos said.

Despite his fascination with the South Pole, he has not yet travelled to the continent.

"I've written about it so often, but always from my desk - this is quite the incentive to go and visit.

"Antarctica is the front line of the biggest news story on planet Earth - climate change," he added.

The naming of geographical features in Antarctica follows strict rules.

The Amos Channel was recommended by the UK Antarctic Place Names Committee, which looks after names for sites within the British Antarctic Territory, as well as South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

Athena Dinar, from the British Antarctic Survey, said: "Jon's passion for Antarctica and engaging journalism offers something for every reader, viewer or listener.

"The naming of an Antarctic place in his honour is a fitting recognition of his outstanding contribution to the promotion of Antarctic research."

Amos joined the BBC in 1986 as a local radio reporter in Cambridge. He was part of the team that launched the BBC News website in 1997, and ran the online science desk for many years. He later worked as a BBC science correspondent across TV, radio and online, before leaving the organisation in 2024.

"Jon consistently highlighted the importance of Antarctic research, explaining not only what science is being done there, but why it matters for society, climate understanding and the global environment," said Fiona Fox, from the Science Media Centre.

articles.title: Maharashtra recorded eight farmer suicides a day on average from Jan 2022 till June 2026: RTI
articles.summary: Maharashtra logged 13,128 farmer suicides from Jan 2022–Jun 2026 (8/day average); RTI alleges govt withheld district-wise data; 7,850 families got Rs 1 lakh.
articles.body: Mumbai: Maharashtra recorded 13,128 farmer suicide cases between Jan 2022 and June 2026 — averaging more than eight a day — but it has withheld district-wise figures sought under the Right to Information (RTI) Act, activist Jeetendra Ghadge has alleged.The relief and rehabilitation department’s figures show that 8,145 cases were found eligible for govt assistance, 4,042 were rejected as ineligible and 941 remain under inquiry. Of the eligible cases, 7,850 families have received Rs 1 lakh each, while 295 are still awaiting payment.Ghadge, of the Young Whistleblowers Foundation, had sought district-wise and month-wise figures for the 54-month period. On July 24, the department’s public information officer, Snehal Sawant, said the information was available with individual district collector offices and advised him to approach them. Ghadge filed a first appeal on Aug 18. After a hearing on Sept 8, the department provided a consolidated statewide table but did not disclose the district-wise breakdown.The missing data are crucial for identifying clusters of distress, comparing trends across districts and assessing whether govt interventions are working, he said.Ghadge’s demand for wider financial protection dates back to June 21, 2023, when he wrote to then chief minister Eknath Shinde about families whose Rs 1 lakh compensation claims had been rejected. articles.title: 'Travesty of justice': SC flays UP Police for 'slipshod probe' in murder case, orders reparation for undertrial
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the Uttar Pradesh government to pay Rs 6 lakh in reparation to a man who spent six years in jail as an
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the Uttar Pradesh government to pay Rs 6 lakh in reparation to a man who spent six years in jail as an undertrial in a murder case before being acquitted. The apex court said that the years lost to a faulty investigation were a travesty of justice.Slamming the state police for a “slipshod investigation” and the prosecution for its haphazard handling of the case, a bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran called the man a “victim of the system”. It said six years of his life had been erased based on a “concocted story” built on mere surmises and conjectures.The man had been in custody since November 14, 2019, in a murder case registered in Agra.The Supreme Court noted that the trial court acquitted him after finding that none of the four circumstances cited by the prosecution, including electronic evidence, had been proved.“This is a classic case of how an investigation should not be proceeded with, resulting in the prosecution putting into jeopardy a person's life and liberty,” the bench said.The court directed the state to pay the compensation within one month, acknowledging that the amount was small compared with the years he had spent behind bars.“We, hence, direct the state to pay an amount of Rs 6 lakh; though paltry in comparison to the years spent in custody, within a period of one month to the petitioner herein,” it said.The verdict came on a plea challenging an Allahabad High Court order in January that had denied the man bail. The Supreme Court had directed the trial court on March 23 to conclude the proceedings within three months. The trial was subsequently completed, and the accused was acquitted.The bench said the case highlighted the failure of investigating and prosecuting agencies to safeguard an individual's liberty despite the presumption of innocence.“The state cannot shirk from its responsibility to protect its citizens, especially when a person arraigned in a criminal case is presumed innocent until proven guilty,” it said.The court stressed that the role of investigating and prosecuting agencies was not simply to secure convictions, but to ensure justice for all parties, including the accused.“They should recognise themselves to be essential stakeholders in the justice delivery system, ensuring justice, not only to the victim, the de facto complainant and the injured, but also to the accused,” the bench said.The judges also expressed concern over the wider implications of such cases, saying they had encountered similar failures but that this one stood out for its severity.“We come across such travesty of justice in many matters, but in some, so blatant and shocking, as in this case, which requires reparation to the accused, who in turn is a victim of the system,” it said.The bench directed that a copy of its verdict be sent to the Uttar Pradesh director general of police and the state's home secretary. It also urged the police to train officers in proper investigative procedures, criticising the manner in which the case had been handled.The court said the acquittal was fortunate, given the consequences of the flawed investigation and prosecution for the man's life and liberty.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
